A coalition of organizations is calling on the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) to extend its telemedicine prescribing flexibilities deadline given the lack of finalization to a key rule.

The flexibilities are set to expire on Dec. 31, and the agency’s Special Registrations for Telemedicine and Limited State Telemedicine Registrations final rule has not been published.

The coalition said patients and providers are “facing unacceptable uncertainty and the real risk of care disruptions,” noting that providers and platforms will need time to review requirements and apply for registration even if the rule is published in November.

Advocates are calling for an extension through at least Dec. 31, 2027.

#5724. RFK Jr. Is Ushering in Peptides. As an Oncologist, Here Are My Concerns.

— Clinical evidence hasn't caught up with commercial enthusiasm

On July 13, 2025, at a Las Vegas hotel hosting the Revolution Against Aging and Death Festival, two women were taken away in ambulances. Both had received injections containing experimental peptides at a conference booth. Both became seriously ill and required ventilators. One mixture was believed to contain MOTS-c, P21, BPC-157, and TB4, substances promoted for tissue repair, metabolic health, and longevity.

Both women recovered. Nevada regulators subsequently imposed $35,000 in fines on four parties involved. But investigators could not establish what caused the reactions. They were unable to obtain the injected products for laboratory testing, and their exact contents remain unverified.

That is what bothers me most: two women experienced life-threatening reactions, and investigators could not determine precisely what they received.

Now, Washington is opening a regulatory path for some of these unproven peptides. On October 28, HHS announced an interim enforcement-discretion policy covering six peptides: BPC-157, MOTS-c, TB-500, KPV, Semax, and Epitalon. Under specified conditions, the government does not intend to take enforcement action against licensed pharmacies and physicians compounding these substances while the FDA considers formal rulemaking.

This is not an FDA approval, and it does not establish safety or effectiveness. While the HHS policy includes safeguards that represent progress, the policy also permits wider access before clinical evidence has caught up with commercial enthusiasm.

The question is not whether peptides have therapeutic potential. Many of them do. The question is whether that potential justifies their use before we know whether they work and are safe. The policy followed a July meeting of the FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee, which voted eight to six with one abstention, to recommend BPC-157 for the compounding list. It also endorsed five of the other six substances considered.

FDA reviewers had reached a different conclusion. Their briefing documents found insufficient evidence to support adding any of the seven substances. For BPC-157, evaluated for ulcerative colitis, they could not establish effectiveness. For several others, including TB-500, KPV, MOTS-c, and Epitalon, human safety studies were absent or extremely limited. Reviewers also identified problems with product characterization.

I have spent much of my career conducting oncology trials, including studies contributing to immunotherapies and targeted agents that are now used worldwide. I have seen promising mechanisms fail to translate into patient benefit and unexpected toxicities emerge after treatments entered routine practice. Clinical development is slow, expensive, and often disappointing. But it is how we distinguish a promising hypothesis from a useful medicine. We should make the review process more efficient, not bypass it.

I see a particular oncologic concern with the premature movement on peptides. Experimental studies suggest BPC-157 may stimulate angiogenesis, the formation of new blood vessels, through pathways involving VEGFR2 and endothelial nitric oxide synthase. Angiogenesis supports normal tissue repair. It is also a process many tumors exploit to sustain growth. This does not mean BPC-157 causes cancer or promotes tumor progression -- we lack human evidence to make that claim. But neither can we definitively exclude such effects, particularly with prolonged exposure or in patients with existing or previously treated malignancies.

In oncology, we routinely encounter treatments acting on pathways shared by normal and malignant tissues. Biological activity beneficial in one setting may have unintended consequences in another. The response should not be to assume harm, but to investigate it.

There is also an indication mismatch. The FDA evaluated BPC-157 for ulcerative colitis, while much commercial interest concerns tendon injuries, exercise recovery, and anti-aging. Evidence for one indication cannot establish safety or effectiveness for another, particularly when doses, routes, and duration differ.

The HHS policy includes safeguards worth acknowledging: appropriately sourced ingredients, documentation of identity and purity, single-ingredient preparations, labeling, serious adverse-event reporting, and patient-specific prescriptions. These address genuine problems in the existing peptide market. Patients already obtain experimental substances through poorly regulated online suppliers. Licensed compounding under defined conditions could reduce some risks.

But we must distinguish between three questions:

Manufacturing controls help answer the first one. Toxicology and clinical studies address the second. Well-designed trials establish the third. A certificate of analysis cannot demonstrate effectiveness. A prescription does not establish a favorable benefit-risk ratio. Adverse-event reporting cannot replace prospective safety studies.

Compounding serves an important clinical purpose, meeting individual needs when commercial formulations are unsuitable. But it should not replace drug development. When experimental peptides are marketed through wellness clinics, telehealth, and social media to thousands of patients for similar purposes, they begin to resemble commercial drugs, even when prescriptions are individualized.

The same principle applies to longevity medicine. Research into cellular senescence, mTOR signaling, metabolic regulation, and cellular reprogramming offers genuine opportunities. I welcome it. But results in mice do not establish human benefit, and widespread use without systematic study does not necessarily generate reliable knowledge. We should accelerate research, not replace it with uncontrolled experimentation.

The HHS policy remains interim, with public comments invited through November 13. That process should address dosing, clinical benefit, long-term safety, adverse-event surveillance, and opportunities to link expanded access to systematic evidence generation.

The choice is not between innovation and regulation. Good regulation enables innovation while protecting patients from uncertain benefits and risks. We have learned this repeatedly in cancer drug development: a compelling mechanism begins a research program. It does not prove a drug is effective.

Innovation deserves encouragement. And patients deserve evidence.

The first thing that comes to mind when you mention Quattro is probably Audi's 1980 Group B rally car. It makes perfect sense that the German manufacturer would lean on that legacy when promoting its new Q7 and SQ7 SUVs that have the trademarked all-wheel-drive system, but the company did something much cooler for its new ad campaign: Audi reunited Michèle Mouton with a Quattro S1 at the iconic Pikes Peak hill climb. The 1982 World Rally Championship runner-up still looked at home behind the wheel of the 493-horsepower rally monster.

Audi's new ad campaign titled "Performance Runs in the Family" features a pair of videos: a typical 30-second TV spot, and a 4-minute short with Mouton driving a Quattro S1 up Pikes Peak. During the visually stunning drive up the Colorado mountain, she reminisced about the animosity she faced during the 1985 hill climb, her winning run, and how the ascent has changed in the 41 years since.

Mouton was the first woman and the first non-American to win the Pikes Peak International Hill Climb. The Frenchwoman set a record time of 11:25.390 up the treacherous 12.4-mile ascent, besting the previous record set by Al Unser Jr. in 1983 by 13 seconds. Mouton is still effortlessly cool, still delivering pointed one-liners as naturally as the rest of us breathe. During the revival run, she noted, "When I was at this spot in the race, I had no time for feelings."

The 30-second TV spot mixes archival footage of Mouton during the Group B era with footage of a 2027 Audi SQ7 driving up Pikes Peak. To emphasize the campaign's legacy theme, the ad features Mouton alongside her daughter, Jessica. The SUV's new styling looks just as aggressive and far more comfortable for a family. Vito Paladino, Audi of America's President, stated in a release:

"Audi's story of quattro didn't end with rally racing. That connection between performance and everyday capability is what makes quattro such a defining part of our brand. The all-new Audi Q7 family carries that legacy forward, bringing together Audi's performance heritage with the innovation and engineering that define the next generation of our vehicles."

The 1985 Pikes Peak International Hill Climb was Mouton's last event with Audi before she departed for her farewell season with Peugeot. The Frenchwoman and her accomplishments will forever be tied to Audi. Mouton's four WRC victories with the Audi Quattro are a legacy every four-wheel-drive model produced by the German automaker inherits. It's not merely laurels to rest on, but a level of performance that Audi has to honor.

#5722. Science For The People, Right On!

Today United for the Future launches at COP31 today with a plan to unite 100 million people in peaceful, non-partisan marches in cities worldwide. Their goal is to assemble the largest coordinated climate demonstration in history in order to put climate action back at the top of the political agenda.

Backers of the initiative include Christiana Figueres, former UN climate chief and a key architect of the Paris Agreement; Bill McKibben, author and co-founder of 350.org; Ram Ramanathan of Scripps Institution of Oceanography, UC San Diego; and Sandrine Dixson-Declève, honorary president of the Club of Rome.

Together, they beckon citizens around the world: “Protect our future. Act on the science.” Their call asks governments to stop weakening climate protections and to deliver action that cuts emissions and protects nature in line with science.

Limiting temperature rise to a 1.5 degrees Celsius, or 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit, above the preindustrial levels of the early 1800s was a goal established during the 2015 Paris Agreement. Since then, it’s been a focus of international climate negotiations, and one that’s often been politically contentious.

“For too many people, climate change is deadly,” UN climate chief Simon Stiell said at COP31. “At this COP, nations face a choice: electric or shock. Rewire the global economy for the electric age. Or accept ongoing fossil fuel cost pain for families, firms, and governments.”

Global carbon emissions from fossil fuels are projected to decrease by 0.4% in 2026, driven by expansion of solar and wind power and the Iran conflict, according to new research by the Global Carbon Project.

Then there’s the recent blue tsunami that took place in the US midterm elections, which served as a condemnation of the Trump administration. Historian and activist Rebecca Solnit exclaims, “It was a dam breaking, the dam that held back the will of the people, the people of the world’s most diverse country, the people who believed in their own rights and equality and in the rights and equality of others.”

Now, through promised agendas to increase affordability for consumers, Democrats have a keen opportunity to foreground science as a way to accomplish goals. Senator Bernie Sanders (I-VT) admonishes the new Democratic majority to deliver on its campaign jargon. “No more empty rhetoric. No more telling us how terrible Trump and the Republicans are. No more excuses,” he says. “We now have the votes to pass legislation that will demonstrably improve the lives of millions of working families. And that’s what we must do.”

Sanders insists that the time is now to “act boldly.” Democrats can create millions of good-paying jobs, he continues, “by moving our energy systems away from fossil fuels to energy efficiency and sustainable energy.”

David Fickling outlines in Bloomberg this week that renewables have already made tremendous headway, to the point that “sometimes, change comes at you so fast that you forget to congratulate yourself on what you’ve achieved.”

In 2025 clean energy sources generated nearly the same amount of electricity as the entire world consumed in 1996. About half of that electricity, Fickling continues, was sourced from wind and solar power.

“Instead of concentrating on squeezing the final tons of carbon from electricity,” he offers, “governments need to make abundant clean power cheap enough to drive fossil fuels out of everything else — in particular, electric cars and trucks, home heating systems, and the sort of low-temperature heat used in food and paper manufacturing.”

In that new cohort of leaders is William Lawrence, co-founder of the climate action movement, Sunrise. The Michigan Democrat flipped a House seat and sees clean energy as a way to fulfill campaign promises.

He describes clean energy tax credits as a good place to start.

“It’s a huge issue not just for the climate, but for our energy security,” he states. Climate is as important to energy security as it’s ever been, he tells Claire Brown of the New York Times.” People are experiencing the rising costs of fuel due to the war and volatility around the world. And we can all see the value of being able to have cheap, clean renewable energy that doesn’t depend on the global commodity markets.”

Several scientists and physicians were elected to the US Congress as part of the reinvigoration of science at the federal level. “The importance of having scientists, engineers, and health professionals in national, state, and local political positions cannot be overstated,” relates Deborah D. Stine, the executive director of the President’s Council of Advisers on Science and Technology during the Obama administration. “If the policy question is outside their own expertise, they know how to call on the best experts.”

The incoming scientists represent “a real repudiation of what has been two terrible years for science and public health,” Shaughnessy Naughton, president of 314 Action, chronicles for Alexander Nazaryan of the New York Times.

Where will the US Congress go from here? Rebecca Solnit muses, “What comes after hope, when hope is realized, when hope is no longer necessary?”

Clean energy expert Steve Hanley has an answer to that question. “The guiding star for all policy decisions going forward should be reducing carbon and methane emissions.”

Did you know that electric motors convert 90% of the energy they consume into motion, while an internal combustion engine converts less than 30%? Not everyone is aware of the efficiency of electrifying everything, though. Some scientists are already talking about the important need to draw in a new generation of clean energy advocates among Republicans in Congress and everyday life.

“In almost all circumstances, electrification is a good thing,” says Chris Bowen, Australia’s minister of climate change and energy and COP31’s president of negotiations.

Now we’ll see if Congress can translate political subterfuge into clean energy reality.

#5721. NASA Pushes Further Ahead With The Non-Space Side Of Its Mission, Teases New Experimental Plane

NASA has unveiled, sort of, its newest experimental plane. And by that, the agency appears to mean a plane meant to conduct experiments, rather than the plane itself being the experiment. Called the X-70 Fractal, the aircraft's primary selling point is its modular design, both inside and out. This means that payloads can be swapped out easily, whether they are hanging off the wings or nestled inside the plane. Even the flight controls can be reconfigured in case the agency wants to test different ways for the pilots (and it is piloted) to maneuver. The X-70 is really a platform to allow for a wide array of experiments on a single airframe, rather than creating a bespoke airframe to conduct one mission, like the X-59 is doing now.

As for the plane itself, the X-70 Fractal is... well, more announcement than vehicle, at least for now. NASA says that it can carry 2,000 pounds of science equipment and take off with up to 10,000 pounds total. It will fly up to 45,000 feet in altitude, far above most airliners and well into the stratosphere. It will go up to 1,500 nautical miles, broadly on par with an F-35. It also looks like an F-35, I think, maybe? For images, all we've got is this misty photo that looks AI generated. NASA seems to want to copy the energy of the F-47 and F/A-XX reveals, which are also foggy renderings and not actual photographs. Show me you're making an airplane without showing me you're making an airplane, I guess.

NASA achieves such historic feats in space that it's easy to forget that it is also an "Aeronautics" administration. Part of its remit is to push forward the boundaries of aviation here on this planet, which NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has renewed focus on. Isaacman himself is a pilot who owns his own MiG-29 Soviet fighter jet, so this is an area of personal interest for him. In fact, he's promising that more experimental aircraft are on their way; rumors abound that the agency may be returning the famous SR-71 Blackbird, the fastest plane ever made, to service.

By doing so, NASA does important R&D on airplane technology that is then released into the public record, to the benefit of all aviation companies and everyone who flies on their products. That's the whole point of the X-59, which is trying to reduce the impact of sonic booms enough to make commercial supersonic planes financially viable. In addition, NASA's latest budget points to aviation as an area of strategic competition, per Wired. To that end, it may do some research alongside the Pentagon as well. This is where something like the X-70 is useful: it could do scientific, commercial, or military research as needed, simply by swapping out equipment payloads via its modular design. Now all NASA needs to do is, you know, build it, possibly with a contractor. Details!

Doximity expands clinical AI footprint to more than 190 health systems" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Doximity is rapidly expanding its clinical AI footprint with health systems, with more than 190 organizations having now purchased its AI suite, up from 165 organizations last quarter.

Those health system customers include 10 of the nation's top 20 hospitals, Doximity executives said during the company's fiscal 2027 second-quarter earnings call on Thursday.

NewYork-Presbyterian has integrated Doximity’s AI tools directly into its electronic health record (EHR) workflow. The partnership grants clinicians across NewYork-Presbyterian, Columbia University Irving Medical Center and Weill Cornell Medicine frictionless access to AI tools, including Doximity Scribe and Doximity Ask, the company's AI-powered clinical decision support tool.

NewYork-Presbyterian rolled out Doximity’s AI suite to clinicians across 10 hospitals and hundreds of locations. The deployment builds on NYP’s use of Doximity for video and phone visits since 2021.

UCSD Health is one of the first hospitals to adopt Doximity's new patient context feature, which allows AI to ingest EHR charts, labs, and patient history directly to give patient-specific answers and guideline-based treatment plans, Jeff Tangney, Doximity CEO, said during the earnings call.

"Our patient context feature is now available for thousands of doctors, and they're writing prompts half as long, 12 words versus our 24-word average, because they no longer have to retype the chart details into a search bar. Our AI already has the labs, notes, and problem list, so it can find the pertinent clinical details deep in their record," Tangney said.

The company is also opening API access to its clinical intelligence layer to expand to more workflows.

Tangney stressed that Doximity is focused on offering clinicians a full clinical AI suite across workflows including telehealth, AI documentation, scheduling, clinical questions, patient context and clinical evidence.

"We offer them a suite, not a search bar," Tangney said. "That suite allows them to do the telehealth visit, to have notes taken on that visit, what we call Scribe, and then to ask questions about that visit with the patient context."

Doximity is a digital platform for U.S. medical professionals that offers workflow tools such as a telehealth solution, a clinician-to-patient dialer tool and digital faxing capabilities. The company aims to become a leading AI platform for doctors with plans to scale its clinical AI suite, including its ambient note-taking tool Scribe and clinical AI assistant and medical search engine Ask. A year ago, Doximity acquired clinical AI company Pathway and then integrated Pathway's datasets and its AI into its free Doximity GPT product to offer DoxGPT (now Ask).

Doximity is leaning hard into AI accuracy and safety as AI adoption rapidly grows. AI accuracy "is the number one concern doctors have about AI," Tangney told investors and analysts on the call. "AI deals in probabilities. Patient care demands precision," he said.

The company is making clinical reliability a major part of its competitive positioning. Doximity recently launched DoseCheck, a deterministic verifier for medication safety. Through a partnership with Wolters Kluwer Health, the company embedded UpToDate's evidence-based clinical content directly within Doximity Ask.

"Every clinical AI model has read the National Library of Medicine, which has all of the journals and guidelines, but Wolters Kluwer's UpToDate stands alone as the proprietary gold standard reference for point of care. Their 7,600 physician authors provide unique advice about what to do when there is not an RCT, or randomized controlled trial, to answer the question," Tangney said.

The partnership with UpToDate represents a "strong synergy of Doximity's AI evidence tools and [UpToDate's] unique expert opinion and physician expertise," he noted.

UpToDate has 2,500 health systems as clients, compared to Doximity's 190, and that creates "additional synergies" for the company, Tangney said. Doximity plans to expand its relationship with UpToDate, he noted: "It's the beginning of what we think will be a very strategic, long-term partnership," he added.

Physician AI engagement is growing quickly, according to the company.  Doximity said quarterly active workflow prescribers increased 34% year over year, accelerating from the prior quarter. Approximately half of the 1.8 million U.S. prescribers, roughly 900,000 clinicians, used Doximity workflow products during the quarter. The company sees continued growth in telehealth and scheduling alongside rapidly expanding use of AI and patient-specific clinical tools, Tangney said.

A year ago, the company's workflow active-user growth was in the single digits versus 34% now, Matt Sonefeldt, Doximity's chief financial officer, said during the call. Doximity is investing heavily in AI. Rapid growth in clinician engagement, particularly with the company's workflow tools, is laying the groundwork for greater monetization and business growth over the next several years, Sonefeldt said.

Doximity reported $174.5 million in revenue during the quarter ending September 30, up 4% year over year, beating guidance. Adjusted EBITDA was $89 million, or a 51% margin, despite AI spending growing more than sixfold year over year.

The company reported net income of $34.7 million, versus $62.1 million a year ago, representing a margin of 19.9%, versus 36.8%. And the company reported adjusted EPS of 36 cents per share.

The company's Q2 results beat Wall Street analysts' estimates as analysts expected revenue of $170.8 million, adjusted EBITDA of $81 million and adjusted EPS of 35 cents per share.

Doximity raised its full-year revenue outlook to $678 million to $683 million, about 6% growth at the midpoint. For the full year, the company expects adjusted EBITDA between $317 million and $325 million.

The company launched its commercial AI Search product for pharmaceutical companies in late April, and it's gaining traction with pharmaceutical advertisers, executives said. Sixteen of the top 20 companies have purchased it, with three more in contracting, and bookings have reached eight figures, Sonefeldt said. AI Search revenue will ramp up gradually through calendar 2027, he noted.

AI monetization is coming from the pharma side and selling AI Search as an advertising product, Sonefeldt noted. "We do sell AI as a separate enterprise agreement to health systems customers. We charge a nominal amount as part of our broader workflow suite. As we think about this going forward, we see the primary monetization engine being on the pharma side of our business, specifically through the ad products that we sell," he told analysts during a Q&A on the call.

On the clinical side, Doximity aims to build a trusted AI workflow layer that physicians use for documentation, clinical questions, patient-specific decision support, telehealth and communication. On the commercial side, the company sees opportunities to turn that engagement and clinical intent into a new advertising and search business serving pharma.

"With AI Search now available to our pharma clients, we're growing into a much larger market," Tangney told analysts and investors. "We think we're entering a whole new market here, which has historically been paid search."

Doximity is trying to capture marketing dollars that historically went to Google and other search channels. Tangney cited an estimated $14 billion spent annually by pharma on paid search in the U.S.

The company also plans to introduce biddable or auction-based purchasing, which would make the product look much more like conventional paid search.

Shares of Doximity slumped following its Thursday evening earnings report as investors reacted to significant margin compression, Yahoo Finance reported. Doximity's stock is down nearly 25% this year.

"On the stock, while shares have shed roughly a quarter of value year-to-date due to lingering questions about AI threats and the uncertain backdrop for pharma marketing spend, solid results such as these, along with positive commentary around macro factors should continue to power the recovery that has been ongoing since the fiscal first-quarter earnings print," Ryan Daniels, group head of healthcare technology and services at William Blair, wrote in an analyst note.

"We continue to be optimistic on Doximity's competitive position, with robust growth in utilization metrics and novel AI offerings launching to pharma partners. Continued development of AI-based workflow solutions should support Doximity’s ability to remain a share gainer in healthcare professional (HCP) marketing, supporting long-term growth above market averages," Daniels wrote.

#5719. Cutaneous Sarcoidosis Could Soon Get an Effective Therapy

— Drug already approved for dermatomyositis passes phase II test

ORLANDO -- Patients with cutaneous sarcoidosis -- a condition with no very effective therapy -- saw dramatic improvement with the dual-acting TYK2/JAK1 inhibitor brepocitinib (Lisraya) in a small phase II trial.

Patients treated with either of two doses of brepocitinib achieved 22-point reductions in Cutaneous Sarcoidosis Activity and Morphology Instrument-Activity (CSAMI-A) scores after 16 weeks, well above the 5-point threshold for clinical relevance, compared with no decrease at all with placebo, reported Misha Rosenbach, MD, of the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, and colleagues.

The drug also showed strong efficacy for secondary outcomes, the group found, and no serious adverse effects were recorded. The study was published in JAMA Dermatology and was also presented here at the American College of Rheumatology annual meeting.

Cutaneous sarcoidosis might be the biggest treatment challenge in all of dermatology. Corticosteroids have long been the mainstay of therapy, but are only sporadically effective and, among patients who do respond, relapses are common. Second-line treatments such as hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, or tetracyclines don't do much better. Tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors were recommended as third-line therapy in a 2021 treatment guideline, but on very poor evidence. A French case series published in 2017 suggested TNF inhibitors could be used effectively, but the authors noted that adverse effects and discontinuations were common, and one-third of patients relapsed while on therapy.

With this dismal treatment landscape in mind, clinicians have turned to Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors as a possible alternative. Drugs such as tofacitinib (Xeljanz) and upadacitinib (Rinvoq) have been tried with some success, but only in single case reports and small series. Good results were also reported last year with the currently approved TYK2 inhibitor deucravacitinib (Sotyktu) in one patient.

All that bodes well for brepocitinib, which the FDA approved in August for dermatomyositis, and the phase II data in sarcoidosis appear to bear out the promise. Rosenbach and colleagues enrolled 31 patients, randomizing them in a 3:2:2 ratio to 45 or 15 mg/day of brepocitinib or placebo; they could stay on their conventional non-targeted therapies, but oral steroids were withdrawn over the first 8 weeks and topical steroids were stopped at randomization.

Patients were generally in their 40s and 50s. Mean disease duration varied in the three arms: about 10 years for the placebo and high-dose brepocitinib groups, and 4 years in the low-dose group. CSAMI-A scores averaged about 34 at baseline. Roughly 40% of participants had lupus pernio, the lumpy discolored facial and cranial lesions that may be the worst symptom of cutaneous sarcoidosis. Pulmonary sarcoidosis was also common in the sample.

Change from baseline in CSAMI-A score was the primary outcome measure. While no difference between the two brepocitinib doses was seen for this endpoint, "high-bar" outcomes showed some gaps. All patients in the high-dose group saw at least 10-point reductions in CSAMI-A scores, compared with 73% on the low dose (and 14% in the placebo group). Similarly, "functional remission," defined as a score below 5, was achieved by 62% with 45 mg versus 46% on 15 mg, and none receiving placebo.

Perhaps most encouragingly, all five patients in the 45-mg group with lupus pernio achieved 10-point reductions in CSAMI-A scores. Patients on the active drug also had substantial improvement in skin-related quality of life, whereas the placebo group actually had deterioration. (The near-total lack of improvement with placebo for any efficacy outcome testifies to just how difficult cutaneous sarcoidosis is to treat.)

With regard to safety, one patient in each arm quit therapy because of adverse events. But none were rated as serious. One patient on 45 mg showed a creatinine kinase elevation, and one developed anemia. Otherwise, no "special interest" events were seen; these included cardiovascular events, viral reactivation, transaminase elevations, venous thromboembolism, and malignancies.

Following his conference presentation, Rosenbach was asked where brepocitinib might fit in the treatment algorithm for cutaneous sarcoidosis. He cautioned that it was still early to speculate on that, since a larger phase III trial is only just getting underway. But if those data are like those he reported, "I imagine many patients would get it as first line," he said.

He was also asked about effects on pulmonary and joint manifestations, which are common in cutaneous sarcoidosis. He said the studies thus far have really focused on skin, and he couldn't say much about other symptoms. He added, though, that these would almost certainly be examined in the phase III trial.

Brepocitinib's developer, Priovant Therapeutics, expects primary results from the phase III study at the end of 2028. Rosenbach said the 45-mg dose will be the one tested for potential approval. Additional trials are underway in uveitis and lichen planopilaris; there's no indication, however, that Priovant plans to challenge deucravacitinib, which is approved for plaque psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis.

#5718. Scientists discover that some “unhealthy” diets can boost cancer immunotherapy in mice

Scientists have uncovered an unexpected connection between diet and cancer treatment. In a surprising finding, certain diets typically considered "unhealthy" or "fattening" actually improved responses to a common form of cancer immunotherapy in mice.

The discovery suggests that the success of cancer treatment may depend not only on which bacteria live in the gut, but also on the foods that help those bacteria thrive.

"There is a synergistic relationship between the bacteria that reside in our GI tract, and the food we eat," said Daniela Quail, Associate Professor in the Department of Physiology and Principal Investigator at the Rosalind & Morris Goodman Cancer Institute.

"Even with the right composition of bacteria in your gut, the foods you eat to nourish those populations can determine whether or not you respond to treatment," said Quail.

Quail co-led the research, which examined how diet influences the effectiveness of immune checkpoint inhibitors. These widely used immunotherapy drugs help the immune system recognize and attack cancer cells. Other senior researchers involved in the study included McGill scientist Logan Walsh and CR-CHUM collaborators Bertrand Routy and Arielle Elkrief. The findings were published in Nature.

Why Unhealthy Diets Produced Surprising Results

One of the most unexpected discoveries was that some diets associated with weight gain appeared to make immunotherapy more effective, challenging assumptions about the relationship between nutrition and cancer treatment.

"Our findings were surprising because they highlighted a benefit of some obesogenic diets," she said. "That tells us the relationship between diet and cancer treatment is more complex than a simple message to eat healthy and exercise."

However, the researchers emphasize that these results should not encourage cancer patients to consume diets that promote obesity. Excess weight carries established health risks, and the findings do not demonstrate that adopting such diets would improve cancer treatment in humans.

Instead, the scientists want to understand how different foods influence the gut microbiome, the enormous community of trillions of bacteria that inhabit the digestive system. Identifying the mechanisms responsible for the improved treatment responses could eventually help researchers develop safer ways to make cancer immunotherapy more effective.

A New Explanation for Cancer's Obesity Paradox

The investigation grew out of a longstanding puzzle in cancer research known as the "obesity paradox."

Obesity is generally linked to a greater risk of developing cancer and dying from the disease. Yet several studies have found that cancer patients with a higher body mass index (BMI) sometimes respond more favorably to immune checkpoint inhibitors.

To investigate this apparent contradiction, the research team tested 12 different diets in mice. Surprisingly, some diets associated with obesity improved the animals' responses to immunotherapy, even when they were consumed for relatively short periods.

These results suggest that the apparent treatment advantage associated with obesity may not be primarily caused by excess body weight. Instead, the explanation could involve the combined influence of diet and gut bacteria on the immune system.

By uncovering how these interactions affect cancer treatment, researchers hope to identify new approaches that reproduce the beneficial effects without exposing patients to the health risks associated with obesity.

The study, "Diet-microbiome synergy underlies obesity-associated immunotherapy efficacy," was published in Nature by McGill PhD graduate Lysanne Desharnais, Daniela Quail, and their collaborators.

Funding was provided by the Canadian Institutes of Health Research, the Canadian Cancer Society, the Terry Fox Research Institute, the Canada Foundation for Innovation, and philanthropic supporters including La Vie en Rose and the Bachynski Family Foundation.

#5717. DOJ Slaps Lyft With $53 Million Lawsuit For Allegedly Discriminating Against Disabled Riders

The U.S. Department of Justice is suing ride-hailing company Lyft, accusing it of routinely discriminating against people with disabilities in direct violation of federal law. The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, alleges that Lyft and its drivers "routinely refuse to serve" people with disabilities, such as folks who use stowable wheelchairs or ride with service animals. The DOJ also accused the San Francisco–based company of imposing cancellation fees on people who were denied service and charging passengers with disabilities higher fees and unnecessary surcharges.

The Justice Department sought $53 million in damages for the "hundreds, and likely thousands" of customers it said Lyft and its drivers had wronged, and it's the latest in a series of legal actions the government has taken against major ride-hailing companies related to alleged Americans with Disabilities Act violations, according to Reuters. Just last year, the DOJ accused Uber of similar behavior and sought $125 million in damages. Uber says it has since committed to expanding access and improving the experience of riders with disabilities.

The department said Lyft failed to change its policies and practices to prevent this sort of discrimination, and it failed to adequately train drivers and customer service representatives about their obligations under federal law, The New York Times reports. On top of the $53 million in damages for passengers, the government is asking the court to consider a civil penalty against Lyft.

Uber, and now Lyft, have disagreed with the allegations vehemently. Here's what Lyft told The Times in a statement:

Discrimination has no place in the Lyft community. We have longstanding policies requiring drivers to accommodate riders who travel with service animals or use foldable mobility devices, and drivers who violate these policies face serious consequences, including permanent deactivation.

It should be noted that Lyft says it is fully cooperating with the Department of Justice through this entire process.

Unfortunately for everyone involved, this is not the first time Lyft has been in hot water over discriminating against folks with disabilities. As The Times points out, the company resolved allegations that its drivers denied services to people who used wheelchairs or walkers in 2020. Admittedly, the scope and penalties were far smaller back then, but it's a big deal nonetheless. Six years ago, it agreed to revise its policies and pay four passengers thousands of dollars in damages, along with a $40,000 civil penalty.

#5716. Strengthening Healthcare Delivery Through Proactive Primary Care

Strengthening Healthcare Delivery Through Proactive Primary Care" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

A stroke can happen without warning. In the months beforehand, however, there may have been a blood pressure reading that needed attention, a prescription that lapsed or a follow-up visit that never got scheduled. Primary care is usually where those signals surface first, and where there is the best chance to act before an emergency.

Much of that work happens between appointments. Care teams review charts ahead of visits, call patients after a hospital discharge and follow up on overdue screenings. Traditional fee-for-service pays for the visit itself but offers little support for the proactive work around it. Value-based care shifts the focus from the volume of services delivered to the quality, outcomes and total cost of care. By aligning financial incentives with prevention, it helps keep patients healthy and out of the hospital while strengthening the long-term financial sustainability of the practice.

For people with traditional Medicare, the Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP) enables primary care practices to be paid for that preventive work. MSSP is a permanent, voluntary accountable care program run within traditional Medicare by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS). Physician groups, health systems and community health centers participate by joining an accountable care organization (ACO), which takes responsibility for the quality and total cost of care for its assigned patients.

Clinicians continue to bill Medicare for covered services under fee-for-service, and MSSP adds a layer of value-based savings on top. When proactive primary care lowers the total cost of patients' care against a historical benchmark, often by preventing avoidable hospitalizations and emergency visits, and the ACO meets quality standards, Medicare shares a portion of those savings with the ACO. Because savings stem directly from keeping people healthy, clinical goals and financial rewards finally pull in the same direction. Shared savings are not guaranteed and depend on multiple factors.

The program operates at significant scale. In performance year 2026, 511 ACOs are serving 12.6 million people with traditional Medicare.¹ In performance year 2024, 75% of participating ACOs earned shared savings, and the program produced roughly $2.5 billion in net savings for Medicare.²

Physician-led value-based care puts primary care physicians and practices at the center of care delivery and decision-making. Shared savings give primary care organizations a revenue stream tied to prevention, which they can reinvest in staff, outreach and technology.

An ACO enablement partner can provide the data, care model support and operational infrastructure needed to identify patient needs, coordinate care and manage the ACO's reporting to Medicare, while participating primary care organizations retain control over how they deliver care. Aledade is one such partner. In fact, practices with five or more years with Aledade deliver approximately three times higher savings than the national average for non-Aledade ACOs of similar tenure.3

With that support and the actionable insights and clinical guidance it brings, primary care teams can reach the right patient at the right time, and the results show up as an emergency visit avoided, a stroke prevented or a hospital stay that never happened. For patients, prevention can mean more birthdays, more holidays and more time with the people they love.

Aledade is a physician-led value-based care company and the leading value-based care participant in MSSP.4 Aledade works alongside primary care organizations to put proactive care into practice through true financial alignment. Within its ACOs, savings are generally allocated approximately 50% to Aledade and 50% to its practice partners, with individual practice distributions weighted by quality performance and other contractual terms.⁵ That means Aledade succeeds only when its primary care partners do.

For more than a decade, Aledade has partnered with thousands of primary care organizations through the ACOs it forms and manages, providing data, technology, care model support and operational infrastructure. Together, these capabilities help clinicians identify patient needs earlier, coordinate care and build a sustainable financial model that helps direct more revenue to primary care. When primary care is financially incentivized to keep patients healthy, warning signs can be caught earlier and life-threatening events can be prevented.

1 2026 Medicare Accountable Care Organization Initiatives Participation Highlights, CMS.

2 CMS Proposes Transformational Medicare Reforms to Expand Accountable Care, CMS, July 2026.

3 Aledade analysis of CMS Public Use File of MSSP annual results through 2024; for Aledade data incorporates private CMS data for 2025; weighted average of performance for all data 2015+, incorporates Aledade 2016+ cohorts.

4 Based on internal analysis of data from the 2024 CMS ACO Public Use File.

5 Based on Aledade's standard ACO contractual terms as of January 1, 2026.

#5715. At $17,000, Is This Meyers Manx SR2 A Super Cool Cat?

Today's Nice Price or No Dice Manx SR2 is the second VW-based kit car offered by legendary builder Bruce Meyers, and it features a design he thought would be far harder to copy than his first: the ubiquitous dune buggy. Let's decide what such a unique bit of car culture should cost.

With the recent discontinuation of the Supra, fans eager to carry the torch of non-tepid Toyotas are left with only the GR86 coupe and the crazily expensive GR Corolla as rides of choice. The fact that Toyota couldn't be bothered to develop the last-generation Supra on its own, leveraging BMW for most of the under-skirt bits, makes it questionable whether the company even has any interest in sporty cars anymore. Instead of pulse-pumping sports cars, the company offers around a dozen five-door crossover-style vehicles, since that's what sells these days.

That wasn't always the case; in addition to the Supra, Toyota once offered a rally-bred version of the stalwart Celica and a full-blown mid-engine sports car in the MR2. We looked at a 1993 Toyota MR2 on Tuesday, a non-turbo car that otherwise had all the options we'd want. Unfortunately, that non-turbo nature and a non-working A/C compressor called into question its $14,000 asking price. In the end, you all gave that a heave-ho in an 85% 'No Dice' downvote.

A lack of taint-tightening Toyotas doesn't mean that the automotive landscape has totally turned into dullsville, however. There are plenty of fun and interesting cars and, yes, even trucks, out there from which to choose when something more than sleepwalking self-driving is in order. But what if you wanted something crazier than what's on the menu right now from the ever-shrinking cadre of entertaining cars on the market? That's when a rare opportunity like today's Meyers Manx SR feels especially apt.

The SR2's creator, Bruce Meyers, grew up living the California dream. A bohemian artist and engineer, Meyers spent his early adult years surfing, off-road racing, and teaching himself to mold fiberglass as a boat builder. His talents all merged in the creation of the original Meyers Manx dune buggy, introduced in 1964.

Built on a VW Type 1 platform shortened by 14.5 inches, the Manx immediately became an icon and set off an industry of copycats. Meyers went to court to stop the copiers from making dime on his design, but to little success. Taking another tack, Meyers' next street kit, the Manx SR2 (Street Roadster), was far more complex, featuring 10 body panels (as opposed to the original Manx's two) and iconic scissor-style doors. Unfortunately, the cost of the lawsuits, along with nasty letters from the IRS, ate away at Meyers' company finances, and he closed the doors in 1971. By that time, fewer than 200 Manx SR body kits had left the Fountain Valley factory.

This is one of those rare SR models, built on a VW Beetle platform, but powered by a Chevy Corvair air-cooled six. Unlike most automotive engines, the Corvair mill spins counterclockwise, so the car also has the Chevy four-speed manual gearbox instead of a VW transmission. According to the ad, the added power (likely around 140 horsepower gross) makes the car "fly!"

The car rolls, appropriately enough, on a set of Western Bullet Torque Thrust-style wheels wrapped in white-letter BF Goodrich tires. They sit proud in the exaggerated wheel arches, looking almost comically large in comparison to the car's miniature 80-inch wheelbase.

Another way Bruce Meyers and co-designer Stewart Reed sought to improve upon the original Manx was through weather protection, fitting the SR2 with an optional fabric targa top and side curtains. This car appears to have neither, nor does it even seem to have a windshield wiper, making it a fair-weather friend. It's also missing one of the front bumperettes, which could be hard to find. Other than those issues, the car's exterior appears to be in really good shape, with the paint still shining and everything else still intact.

Make no mistake, though: this car is a project that needs some work. The seller claims the seats are "ready for upholstery," implying that they have somehow been pre-gaming for the effort. There's also apparently an issue with the scissor doors (a first, by the way), as they seem to be sitting in place in most of the pictures but aren't actually attached by their hinges. That's evident in the interior photo, where the passenger-side door is absent entirely.

The interior itself is in rough but serviceable condition. Those upholstery-ready seats are nothing more than fiberglass shells with an inch or so of ancient foam padding, and they look about as comfortable as sitting on an orange crate. The rest of the cabin is black-painted fiberglass with a bare VW floorpan. Neither element looks too egregious.

The dashboard offers a full complement of VDO gauges with the tach hilariously pegged at a 4,500 rpm redline. The speedometer's odometer inset shows 30,461 miles, but the ad claims an "I don't know" 99,999 as the mileage. On the plus side, the car's title is clean, and the seller claims it is licensed as an "asvr," which I believe means home-built, with a 1987 VIN assignment.

As noted at the outset, this Manx SR is one of those rare birds to catch in the classifieds. It's not crazy rare, though, as there's another with the same Corvair power, but in orange and with a salvage title, offered through one of the classic car classifieds.

This one, despite some questions and missing pieces, looks like a great foundation for a light restoration. That would result in a unique and fun sport-about for weekend and car show duty. Find the top and side curtains, and rain won't be the hindrance the car currently faces.

With all that in mind—and yes, it was a lot—what do you think about this Manx SR? More importantly, how do you feel about spending $17,000 to buy it? Is that a fair price, given the car's rarity and condition? Or does that price make you want to turn tail and run?

Los Angeles, California, Craigslist, or go here if the ad disappears.

#5714. Closing the last mile of value-based care with AI

Closing the last mile of value-based care with AI" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

One of the most challenging parts of value-based care is its timing. Too often, diagnosis gaps or risks arrive late, after an appointment or follow-up, when there is less opportunity to improve care and results.

This is a persistent last-mile challenge in VBC: translating population-level information into action within everyday workflows. Reports, payer portals, and standalone analytics tools may identify important opportunities, but practices are often left on their own to connect those insights to the clinicians and teams responsible for addressing them.

AI can help close that distance. Instead of simply generating more insights, AI combined with clinical and payer data can surface actionable intelligence at the point in time when teams address care gaps, evaluate diagnoses, and monitor VBC performance.

Put VBC insights where clinicians can act on them

Identifying a potential diagnosis gap is only part of the job. A clinician still needs enough information to determine whether the diagnosis is supported by the patient’s record and, if so, document it appropriately. If finding that evidence requires searching through the chart or consulting a separate tool, a useful insight can create additional work before it leads to action.

The stakes are also rising. As scrutiny of risk-adjustment coding increases, practices need confidence that every documented diagnosis is supported by the record. An AI suggestion surfaced without clearly documented rationale can add risk, instead of the opposite.

This raises the standard for AI in diagnosis-gap workflows. Each suggested gap should come paired with clinical evidence that references relevant lab and imaging results, vital signs, and clinical notes, so that clinicians can quickly evaluate recommendations within the visit time.

athenahealth’s Clinically Inferred Diagnosis Gaps was built around this model. It uses generative AI to analyze existing chart information and surface potential gaps related to the CMS-HCC risk-adjustment model, along with supporting evidence, inside the clinician’s existing workflow.

Bring payer insights into the clinical workflow

With visibility across care settings, payers have a unique line of insight into patients’ overall care journeys. This more comprehensive view may reveal potential diagnosis gaps beyond what a clinician encounters during an individual visit. Bringing those payer-supplied gaps into the clinical workflow can give clinicians additional information to consider while the patient is in front of them.

New workflows connect payer insights with point-of-care clinical actionability. athenahealth’s moment of care diagnosis-gap workflow allows payers to flag a potential diagnosis gap prior to an upcoming appointment, allowing clinicians enough time to review during the encounter. If the clinician determines that a diagnosis is appropriate, they can document it through the existing workflow and can even close the loop by sharing information back to the payer about how the gap was addressed.

Find VBC opportunities across your patient population

For true value at scale, organizations need to be able to look beyond individual patient visits and at their broader populations. Quality and population health leaders need to answer practical questions across entire patient populations: Which patients still have an open care gap? How are clinicians performing on specific quality measures? Where should the team focus its attention next? Getting those answers can require configuring reports, combining results, or exporting data for further analysis.

AI tools offer powerful new ways to facilitate a macro view, plumbing data to surface trends, emerging needs, and risk profiles that can help direct strategies. Rather than requiring users to translate each question into a predefined report, Sage™, athenaOne’s AI assistant, gives them another way to investigate VBC performance and zero in on the patients, clinicians, or measures that need a closer look. For independent practices, that can make population-level information more accessible to the people responsible for turning it into action.

Reduce the work between VBC insight and action

The value-based care burden can be heavy for independent practices with thinner teams and fewer resources. Integrated AI-native platforms with smarter insights, payer data, population analytics, and performance reporting can help practices manage the coordinated efforts required to succeed in VBC.

When these stakeholders and systems can communicate, their independent value becomes exponentially greater. When information is spread across separate reports, payer portals, analytics tools, and clinical systems, practice teams may have to find and reconcile data before they can decide what needs attention.

Bringing more of that intelligence into the environment where clinicians and quality teams already work creates a more direct path: Find an opportunity → add relevant context → get the information to someone who can act → understand performance.

That is the larger opportunity for AI-enabled VBC: not simply generating more information, but making useful clinical, payer, and performance insights easier to put to work.

#5713. A simple blood test could reveal Alzheimer’s risk 10 years before symptoms

A simple blood test could help identify people at increased risk of Alzheimer's-related cognitive decline years before they experience any noticeable problems with memory or thinking. In a large international study, researchers found that older adults with very high levels of a particular blood biomarker faced a 38% chance of developing cognitive impairment within five years. Over 10 years, the estimated risk rose to 78%, although the longer-term findings were based on substantially less data.

The findings offer new insight into the potential of blood tests to predict future cognitive problems in people who currently show no signs of impairment. The research was led by scientists at the Mass General Brigham Neuroscience Institute and involved teams working across three continents. The results were presented at the Alzheimer's Association International Conference and simultaneously published in JAMA.

The study focused on phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217), a blood biomarker associated with Alzheimer's disease. A test measuring this marker recently received federal clearance, raising hopes that blood testing could make Alzheimer's detection more accessible. However, an important question has remained: Can these tests reliably predict whether someone with normal cognitive function will eventually develop symptoms?

Blood Test Reveals Cognitive Decline Risk Years in Advance

To investigate, researchers combined information from six observational studies and clinical trials conducted in North America, Japan, and Australia. Together, these studies included 2,684 older adults who showed no signs of cognitive impairment when they entered the research.

At enrollment, participants provided blood samples that were analyzed for p-tau217. They also underwent positron emission tomography (PET) brain scans, allowing researchers to establish baseline measurements of brain health. Annual follow-up assessments were then used to monitor changes in memory, thinking, and other cognitive abilities.

The combined data covered an unusually long period. Some participants entered one of the studies as early as 2004, while the most recent follow-up assessments took place in 2025.

Across the studies, approximately 478 participants eventually developed cognitive impairment. When researchers compared these outcomes with the original blood test results, they found a strong relationship between higher p-tau217 levels and the likelihood of future cognitive problems.

Among people with very high biomarker levels, the estimated probability of developing cognitive impairment reached 38% within five years. By 10 years, that figure increased to 78%. However, the researchers emphasized that substantially fewer observations were available for the 10-year period and beyond, making those longer-term predictions less certain.

A Powerful Alzheimer's Predictor Beyond Genetics and Brain Scans

One of the most important findings was that p-tau217 provided information about future cognitive decline beyond what could be explained by other established risk factors.

The biomarker remained significantly associated with cognitive impairment even after researchers accounted for amyloid-beta plaques, which are abnormal protein deposits in the brain that can be detected with PET imaging. Its predictive value also extended beyond known genetic risk factors (such as APOE4).

This suggests that a relatively simple blood test could eventually provide doctors with additional information when estimating an individual's likelihood of developing cognitive difficulties.

"This is a critical step toward better understanding what p-tau217 can tell us about a person's risk for cognitive impairment," said lead author Rachel F. Buckley, PhD, a cognitive neuroscientist with the Mass General Brigham Neuroscience Institute. "What really sets this work apart is that it estimates an individual's level of risk for cognitive impairment. We harmonized data across six cohorts, creating a large and varied data set, and still found consistent results showing how p-tau217 informs risk over time."

Rather than simply identifying biological changes associated with Alzheimer's, the research helps estimate how those changes translate into the probability of developing symptoms over a specific period.

Why Alzheimer's Blood Tests Are Not Yet Recommended for Healthy People

Despite the promising results, the researchers caution that blood tests are not currently recommended for routine Alzheimer's risk screening in people without symptoms.

One major reason is that preventive treatments capable of changing the course of the disease have not yet been established for otherwise healthy individuals identified as being at elevated risk.

"We do not yet have disease-modifying treatments for people who find out they are at high risk for developing cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer's disease, which is why we don't recommend currently available blood tests for asymptomatic individuals. Today, our medical advice would remain the same regardless of test results: exercise regularly, maintain a healthy diet, and prioritize sleep and overall wellness," said senior and corresponding author Reisa Sperling, MD, a neurologist with the Mass General Brigham Neuroscience Institute. "But the preventive care landscape could change rapidly if ongoing trials of disease-modifying therapies prove beneficial. In the future, these tests could help identify those who might benefit most from these treatments. Our long-term goal is to get us to where cholesterol testing is in predicting your risk of a heart attack."

There are also important limitations to the research. Although the investigators brought together data from multiple studies and geographic regions, the participants may not fully represent the broader population. This potential selection bias could affect how well the findings apply to other groups.

In addition, the analysis focused on predicting cognitive impairment over relatively limited periods rather than estimating a person's lifetime risk. Researchers say larger, more representative studies and longer follow-up periods will be needed to confirm the findings and improve the precision of individual risk predictions.

Could Blood Tests Help Prevent Alzheimer's Before Symptoms Begin?

The greatest potential benefit of this approach may emerge as scientists develop treatments designed to slow or prevent Alzheimer's-related cognitive decline before noticeable symptoms develop.

Several clinical trials are already investigating whether disease-modifying therapies can benefit people who have biological signs of Alzheimer's but have not yet experienced cognitive impairment. If those treatments prove effective, blood biomarkers such as p-tau217 could help identify individuals most likely to benefit from early intervention.

Such an approach could eventually make Alzheimer's prevention more similar to cardiovascular prevention, where cholesterol measurements help doctors estimate future heart attack risk and determine who may benefit from treatment.

For now, the blood test offers researchers a way to identify higher-risk individuals who may be suitable candidates for prevention studies.

"Today, p-tau217 can help identify people at high risk for future Alzheimer's dementia for participation in prevention trials," said Sperling. "As these trials move forward, individualized estimates, including the biomarker's prognostic value, could guide earlier treatment and monitoring decisions."

Authorship: In addition to Sperling and Buckley, Mass General Brigham authors include Diana L. Townsend, Colin J. Birkenbihl, Madison Cuppels, Gillian T. Coughlan, Mabel T. Seto, Jane A. #5712. Enfortumab Vedotin-Based Treatment Solidified for Muscle-Invasive Bladder Cancer

— Experts discuss survival gains and whether all patients need adjuvant therapy

In this exclusive roundtable video from MedPage Today, three expert leaders in the field of bladder cancer discuss the latest emerging data presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) congress.

Moderator Matthew Galsky, MD, of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City, is joined by David Aggen, MD, PhD, of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York City, and Stephanie Berg, DO, of the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston.

In this first of four episodes, they examine findings from the VOLGA trial, including the survival benefits of enfortumab vedotin (EV; Padcev) plus durvalumab (Imfinzi) and whether all patients need additional treatment following cystectomy.

Following is a transcript of their remarks:

Galsky: Hi everyone. Welcome to MedPage Today ESMO Roundtable on [genitourinary] cancers. And I'm Matt Galsky. I'm a medical oncologist focusing on bladder cancer at the Tisch Cancer Institute at Mount Sinai in New York. And I'm joined today by Dr. David Aggen from Memorial Sloan Kettering and Dr. Stephanie Berg from the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. So welcome both of you. Thanks for joining.

Galsky: Absolutely. We had a pretty consequential set of data from ESMO this year on localized bladder cancer, both muscle-invasive disease and non-muscle-invasive disease. So over the next bit of time, I thought we would talk about some of the more important data, some of the potential practice-changing or practice-informing data, and would love to get your opinion on a set of studies that I think probably are the most important to talk about. And by the end of the discussions, I'm hoping that each of us can identify maybe immediate practice implication related to the data or an unanswered research question that you think should be tackled next.

So I thought we'd start with VOLGA, and I was going to present just a brief overview of the VOLGA study for the audience, and then would love to get your input on VOLGA. So just as a bit of context, we all know that from the KEYNOTE-905 and KEYNOTE-B15 studies in cisplatin-ineligible and cisplatin-eligible patients, respectively, that the regimen of perioperative enfortumab vedotin plus pembrolizumab [Keytruda] with cystectomy is a standard treatment approach for patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer.

VOLGA tested a variation on this theme. So VOLGA enrolled patients who were cisplatin-ineligible or -declining and patients were randomized to receive either cystectomy alone, as was considered a standard of care at the time, or neoadjuvant treatment with enfortumab vedotin plus durvalumab for three cycles and then adjuvant durvalumab.

So a couple of differentiators from KEYNOTE-905: one, the use of durvalumab rather than pembrolizumab. The second is that in the adjuvant phase of treatment, there was no enfortumab vedotin given, which there was in KEYNOTE-905. In this study, it was only adjuvant immune checkpoint blockade. There was a third arm of the study and that included tremelimumab [Imjudo], a few doses of tremelimumab in the neoadjuvant and then one dose in the adjuvant setting, I believe.

The triplet regimen with tremelimumab demonstrated an improvement in disease-free survival, or event-free survival [EFS] rather, but not an improvement in overall survival [OS] -- yet. But the regimen of enfortumab vedotin plus durvalumab showed an improvement in event-free survival and an improvement in overall survival. The hazard ratios look pretty good, 0.51 for OS, 0.58. I'm sorry, 0.51 for EFS and 0.58 for overall survival. And I didn't really comment on the path CR [pathologic complete response] rates in the study, but would love to get your thoughts on that as well.

So Dr. Aggen, what do you think of this study? What does it add to the treatment of patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer?

Aggen: I think that VOLGA really solidifies that enfortumab vedotin with a checkpoint is the standard for patients with muscle-invasive disease. The two phase III trials now in cisplatin-ineligible patients showing a huge benefit in terms of event-free and overall survival to giving neoadjuvant therapy.

I do think a couple key takeaways are that it's unclear the adjuvant contribution of enfortumab vedotin for some patients, and VOLGA really brings that into question, that some patients may not need enfortumab vedotin for an extended course after surgery. It's really on us to figure out who those patients are. There seems to be comparable EFS with a more limited duration of EV therapy.

The second thing though that's sort of of interest is the pathologic complete response rate in VOLGA, which was about 45% by investigator assessment and then closer to 40% actually when it was centrally reviewed. That is slightly lower than what we saw with all the caveats of cross-trial comparisons in EV-303/KEYNOTE-905 and EV304/KEYNOTE-B15.

And so I do think that's something that we're going to be talking about. A key theme of the meeting though in some of the other trials we may discuss later on is that path CR rate doesn't necessarily equate with long-term outcome. There were path CR rates with pembrolizumab in combination with cisplatin on the order of about 44% reported, and that did not equate to the same EFS and OS benefit.

So for me, the key takeaway is that for a patient with muscle-invasive disease, we should be having a conversation about ADC-IO [antibody-drug conjugate and immuno-oncology] therapy. I think that the onus is on us to figure out how much and who needs additional adjuvant treatment based on which regimen you select.

Galsky: Thank you. Dr. Berg, so Dr. Aggen mentioned that not everyone might need adjuvant EV, maybe not everyone needs adjuvant immune checkpoint blockade. Are there criteria that you use in clinic right now to determine what to do after surgery?

Berg: I think right now I'm still using the trial criteria and offering adjuvant, at least immunotherapy, and EV for those I think that can tolerate it. We all know radical cystectomy is quite tough and if you can try to get it in the window of time, but I completely agree with high-risk disease, it's important. But then if they have path CR or low risk, still T1 with a treatment effect, you really question is adjuvant anything needed, especially adjuvant EV.

And when you think about toxicities, like Dr. Aggen mentioned, especially with peripheral neuropathy, thankfully they were getting less EV in VOLGA, just the three cycles, but that can be really life-changing for patients and it's something that we really have to think about. What are we going to be doing for them if we eliminated micrometastasis and increasing that risk for permanent toxicity? So it's something I think the question isn't completely answered, but I think this data really helped at least bridge a little bit of the gap about having a broader discussion about adjuvant EV, and we're going to hopefully see some trials in this space.

And I just wanted to add that this also made me realize, and to tell our patients, that you can still get neoadjuvant treatment and go to surgery. I think it just confirmed that it's not really leading to more complications and it's really established how we're doing, as Dr. Aggen said, EV and ICI [immune checkpoint inhibitor], because I think we're not saying ICI specific now, and I'm sure once NCCN [National Comprehensive Cancer Network] gets a hold of it, we'll have a different wording for that language.

Galsky: Dr. Aggen, what do you make of the CTLA-4 blockade data? Sort of a checkered history in urothelial cancer so far.

Aggen: Unfortunately, it's been difficult to see a clear long-term benefit with CTLA-4 and bladder cancer like we've seen historically in kidney cancer. And it seems that the additional toxicity doesn't necessarily equate to an improvement in terms of pathologic complete response rates and not yet in terms of overall survival. Probably there's a subgroup of patients with immune-infiltrated tumors maybe that could benefit from CTLA-4, but I just don't think we have a clear sense of who those patients are at the moment.

Galsky: Thank you. So maybe one quick take home from both of you regarding VOLGA. How does this impact your practice Monday morning?

Berg: I can go first. I would say it fits in a sense that I'm going to say without cisplatin eligibility, I'm going to offer EV and ICI for patients prior to radical cystectomy if that's what they're choosing for their perioperative care. And that's what I'm going to go with.

Aggen: I think that if 10 years ago, Matt, we told Dean Bajorin that we'd have hazard ratios of 0.51 in muscle-invasive disease, he would've had a hard time believing us. I think that VOLGA reaffirms that ADC-IO therapy is the backbone of neoadjuvant therapy. And there's going to be, I think, a lot of shared decision making when it comes to adjuvant therapy. Certainly for patients with residual disease at cystectomy, those are patients who in my mind absolutely should continue ADC-IO therapy postoperatively.

Galsky: And I think you make a great point. We have two contemporary studies now with comparisons of systemic therapy with cystectomy versus cystectomy alone. It's pretty unusual to have that in solid tumors in this age where systemic therapy is integrated into clinically-localized disease across the board. So there's really no surgery-alone trials anymore.

So two contemporary studies both showing marked improvement in outcomes with perioperative systemic therapy. I think that really sort of seals the question about whether or not perioperative systemic therapy is needed in muscle-invasive bladder cancer. So thank you for those comments.

#5710. From Fragmentation to Integration: A New Model for Specialty Care

From Fragmentation to Integration: A New Model for Specialty Care" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Health systems are navigating growing demands with increasingly limited resources. As costs rise and teams are stretched, technology has become essential to helping people work smarter. But technology alone isn’t the answer. Many health systems and specialty care teams are discovering that more tools don’t always mean a more efficient process or better patient outcomes.

Approximately 25% of healthcare spending in the U.S. goes toward administrative expenses. At the same time, 60% of hospitals and health systems use more than 50 software solutions for operations. Yet more technology hasn’t meant less complexity. Care teams still navigate disconnected tools, siloed data, fragmented workflows, and manual handoffs. The opportunity isn’t to add more technology; it’s to make everything work better together.

Health systems want to better manage the specialty patient journey, but administrative burdens get in the way of more coordinated care. What they need is an integrated approach – one that improves patient experiences and outcomes by connecting workflows through technology and adding dedicated human expertise to serve as an extension of existing care teams.

When specialty care teams spend more time navigating processes and technology than focusing on patients, trust erodes, costs rise, and turnover climbs. It also limits teams’ ability to apply the clinical expertise and personalized attention that complex specialty care requires. This friction shows up in three core areas:

The rapid adoption of specialized software and standalone tools for tasks such as scheduling, patient intake, and remote monitoring fragments care delivery. Teams constantly toggle between platforms, manually piecing together a single patient’s record. This can contribute to cognitive overload among care teams, a factor in burnout, and it diverts valuable time and attention from clinical decision-making and personalized patient support that require human expertise.

Point solutions may solve individual challenges, but they often operate in isolation. When systems don’t fully connect, patient information becomes fragmented across applications, leaving specialty care teams without visibility into the full context of a patient’s broader care journey. This can increase the risk of redundant testing, duplicated work, and inaccurate reporting, while making it harder for clinicians to identify when patients may need additional interventions.

The care journey includes multiple critical transitions, from cross-departmental referrals to prescription routing to external coordination. Despite healthcare’s digital process, these transitions still rely too frequently on faxes, phone calls, and manual spreadsheets. The added administrative burden makes it harder for care teams to coordinate timely interventions and provide consistent, personalized support. Without an integrated model that connects the entire care journey, referrals or post-procedure care plans can fall through the cracks.

Complexity comes at a cost: time teams could be spending on patient care. According to AMA research, for every hour physicians spend with patients, they spend nearly two more on EHR and desk work.

For specialty care teams, disconnected technology and fragmented workflows can make it even harder to see the full picture of a patient’s care. Patients with multiple chronic conditions, for example, often see several specialists. When any one of them lacks complete visibility into the patient’s full treatment plan, specialty performance breaks down. The risk of prescribing therapies that shouldn't be combined rises, potentially compromising patient safety and delaying therapy.

Solving today’s specialty care challenges requires more than another point solution. It requires a connected operating model that brings workflows, information and expertise together, giving care teams the visibility and support they need to act with greater confidence and keep patients moving forward.

Shields Health Solutions’ integrated care model combines technology, data, and clinical expertise to reduce administrative burden, streamline care coordination, and provide specialty care teams with more time to focus on patients. Rather than relying on technology alone, Shields’ clinical pharmacists and liaisons work as an extension of specialty care teams. They translate insights into action, resolving barriers to therapy, coordinating care, and supporting patients throughout treatment.

That combination of human expertise and connected technology delivers measurable results. With average time to therapy in under 48 hours compared with the seven-to-10-day industry average, Shields’ integrated care model drives connected performance, alleviating operational strain on care teams while improving access to therapy, better patient outcomes, and long-term growth.
