#5650. HHS Vaccine Task Force Misses Report Deadline

— Report is part of an overall strategy to undermine trust in vaccines, say public health advocates

Now that the deadline has passed for an HHS vaccine task force to issue its report on the timing and sequencing of vaccines, public health advocates are concerned about what happens when the report eventually comes out.

"The overarching concern with this report, should it ever materialize, is that it will be more textual squid ink that accomplishes nothing other than reinforcing unfounded doubts about vaccines that have been cultivated by the HHS secretary for decades," Elizabeth Jacobs, PhD, professor emerita of epidemiology and biostatistics at the University of Arizona in Tucson and a founding member of Defend Public Health, said in an email. "In fact, this may be its only real purpose."

The report grew out of an executive order issued Aug. 10 by President Donald Trump. The order directed HHS to, within 90 days, present plans to "offer options to administer core childhood vaccines, starting with MMR [measles, mumps, and rubella], as single vaccines rather than combination products/doses" while still guaranteeing continued availability of combination vaccines, and to "assess the ideal timing and sequencing of all core childhood vaccines and adjust the federal childhood and adolescent vaccine schedule as appropriate based on gold standard science." It also directed the agency to "improve vaccine safety monitoring, transparency, and research."

The focus on the MMR vaccine is particularly unhelpful now, "when we are in the midst of an uncontrolled measles outbreak that is likely to result in the U.S. losing its measles elimination status this week or next," said Jacobs, adding that in a just world, "the focus right now would not be on making it more difficult to complete vaccinations for measles, mumps, and rubella. It would be on rolling out a rigorous public health campaign to ensure that all people in the U.S. are protected with the only measles vaccine we have at our disposal -- the safe and effective MMR vaccine."

Asked Tuesday about the missed deadline, an HHS spokesperson said in an emailed statement that the agency "is actively implementing President Trump's Executive Order on Gold Standard Childhood Vaccine Recommendations. The HHS Task Force on Safer Childhood Vaccines is working to strengthen vaccine safety research, improve transparency, and expand options for American families. This work requires careful scientific review, and HHS remains committed to advancing the President's priorities through gold standard science and informed parental choice."

The process of using a task force to recommend changes to the vaccine schedule does not sit well with the Infectious Diseases Society of America.

"Any changes to vaccine recommendations should be made by a legitimate, legal ACIP [Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices] whose members have the relevant expertise and who have been thoroughly vetted and appointed through the standard process," Amanda Jezek, the society's senior vice president of public policy and government relations, said in an email.

"Changes to the childhood immunization schedule that have previously been proposed by the administration lack scientific justification and would cause significant confusion among clinicians, patients, and families and could jeopardize insurance coverage and access to vaccines," she said. "Some of the vaccines that have been discussed to be offered separately are not even manufactured as separate vaccines and there is no scientific justification to separate them."

The task force is just part of a plan by HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to undermine vaccines, Paul Offit, MD, director of the Vaccine Education Center at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, said in a phone interview. "He thinks there's gaslighting, that parents who have seen their children hurt by vaccines are dismissed," he said. "So he's going to get to the bottom of this."

"Kennedy has created a four-pronged initiative that will have an NIH clinic devoted to vaccine safety; that will mine electronic medical records to try and find data showing that vaccines are causing harm; that will pay doctors to report harms to the Vaccines Adverse Event Reporting System [VAERS]; and that will expand [VAERS] and modernize it because he is of the belief that these safety issues are being [hidden], which they're not," said Offit.

"Whenever a vaccine comes into the market, it's very quickly subjected to analysis through vaccine safety data," specifically through the CDC's Vaccine Safety Datalink, he said. "You see who's gotten vaccines and who hasn't, and you can very quickly determine whether there's a problem." For example, that system helped public health researchers figure out that the COVID vaccine caused myocarditis in rare cases.

Offit also scoffed at the idea of paying doctors to report vaccine adverse events -- "as if that's the only way they'd be motivated to do it."

He predicted that eventually, Kennedy "will do the same thing as when he testified at the Senate HELP [Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions] Committee ... he held up a paper that had never been published [because] it was horribly flawed and horribly confounded. And he said, 'Look, here's a paper that shows, using the Florida Medicaid data system, that vaccines cause permanent neurological harm.'"

Under the current plan, Kennedy will point to a series of studies to say, "I was right all along," Offit said. Under a worst-case scenario, "he will try and add some of these harms to the Vaccine Injury Compensation Program. ... If he does that, if he breaks the vaccine compensation program, we'll be right back to where we were in the 1980s when companies left the [vaccine] business."

#5647. Experts say high blood pressure guidelines are missing half the equation

For decades, one of the most common recommendations for lowering high blood pressure has been simple: eat less salt. But a new scientific report suggests that this advice may be missing an equally important part of the equation.

Researchers say that increasing potassium intake, rather than focusing only on reducing sodium, could lead to better blood pressure control. By addressing both nutrients together, this approach could strengthen efforts to prevent hypertension and reduce the risk of serious cardiovascular problems.

The potential impact is enormous. High blood pressure, also known as hypertension, affects more than 1.28 billion adults worldwide and is a major risk factor for cardiovascular disease, including heart attacks and strokes. Although public health recommendations have traditionally emphasized cutting sodium, researchers now argue that getting enough potassium deserves just as much attention.

Sodium and potassium are essential minerals that help regulate fluid balance, nerve signaling, and muscle function. Both also influence blood pressure, but they affect the body in different ways.

Eating too much sodium can cause the body to retain additional fluid, increasing the pressure inside blood vessels. Potassium helps counter some of sodium's effects by supporting the kidneys in removing excess sodium through urine. It also contributes to the normal functioning of blood vessel walls, which plays an important role in maintaining healthy blood pressure.

In a new report, physicians and health experts argue that dietary recommendations should address these two minerals together. Rather than treating sodium reduction as the primary solution, they propose combining it with greater potassium consumption to achieve stronger results.

"It is time to view dietary interventions holistically because food components interact and physiology is integrative across systems," said Naomi Fukagawa, M.D. Ph.D., professor of medicine emerita at the Robert Larner, M.D. College of Medicine at the University of Vermont and first author on the report. "Growing evidence shows that increasing dietary potassium as well as reducing sodium intake work together to better manage hypertension."

A Major Rethink of Blood Pressure Guidelines

The report, published in the peer-reviewed American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, was supported by the IAFNS Sodium in Food and Health Implications Committee.

The researchers examined the scientific evidence underlying current sodium and potassium recommendations, along with practical ways to reduce sodium consumption and increase potassium intake. They also explored the obstacles to implementing these changes and identified areas where additional research and updated public health policies could help improve outcomes.

One of the central concerns is that many people consume too much sodium while getting nowhere near enough potassium. Both dietary patterns can contribute to elevated blood pressure, making them important targets for prevention and treatment.

Despite widespread efforts to encourage people to limit salt, average sodium consumption continues to exceed recommended levels. Meanwhile, potassium intake remains "far below optimal levels in both developed and developing nations," according to the authors.

This imbalance suggests that focusing primarily on what people should eat less of may be overlooking an important opportunity to improve cardiovascular health by encouraging them to consume more of a beneficial nutrient.

Potassium is naturally present in many familiar foods, including fruits, vegetables, legumes, and dairy products. Bananas, potatoes, beans, leafy greens, and yogurt are examples of foods that can help increase potassium intake.

Another possibility is replacing some sodium chloride, the main ingredient in ordinary table salt, with potassium salts. These substitutes can help reduce sodium while simultaneously increasing potassium, potentially addressing both dietary goals at once.

However, creating these products presents challenges for food manufacturers. Adding too much potassium salt can produce an unpleasant metallic taste, limiting how much can be used without affecting flavor. Manufacturers must therefore find a balance that improves nutritional content while keeping foods appealing to consumers.

Increasing potassium is also not appropriate for everyone. People with kidney disease or those taking certain medications may have difficulty regulating potassium levels, so potassium supplements and potassium-based salt substitutes should be used with medical guidance when these concerns apply.

A New Strategy for Fighting High Blood Pressure

The researchers emphasize that reducing sodium remains essential. Their proposal is not to abandon existing advice, but to expand it by recognizing that potassium intake is another major factor in blood pressure regulation.

The authors conclude that "dietary sodium reduction is a foundational strategy for hypertension prevention and management. However, new evidence supports a broadening of the current approach that focuses solely on sodium reduction and provides equal emphasis on increasing potassium intake."

For the more than one billion people living with hypertension, this shift in thinking could have significant implications. Instead of concentrating almost exclusively on reducing salt, future dietary recommendations may increasingly emphasize the combined benefits of consuming less sodium and more potassium.

The underlying message is straightforward: better blood pressure control may depend not only on what people remove from their diets, but also on what they add.

Materials provided by University of Vermont. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Digital health and wellness company Hims & Hers tightened its full-year 2026 revenue outlook after missing Wall Street analysts’ revenue and earnings estimates.

Andrew Dudum, co-founder, chairperson and CEO, pointed investors toward the increasing scale of Hims & Hers' pharmacy and lab infrastructure. That growth is driving efficiencies for the company, as is its artificial intelligence-native experience, he said.

“That infrastructure positions us to launch treatments of increasing complexity, including testosterone replacement therapy this quarter and our Peptides Plus offering later this month,” Dudum said.

Peptides have been a focus for the company as of late, with Dudum telling investors last quarter it plans to offer already-permitted peptides, like sermorelin and NAD+.

Dudum said that Hims & Hers’ long-term strategy focuses on “three critical commitments:” being a leader in metabolic health domestically and globally, leading major markets globally and being "at the forefront of category expansion.”

“Each of these reinforces the other, and together they describe how Hims & Hers becomes the global destination for consumer health,” he said. “We are investing aggressively against all three because this opportunity is growing quickly, and we believe it will become more valuable every quarter.”

The company reported $890.4 million in revenue in Q3, up 49% compared to revenue of $599 million the year prior, according to financial results published Monday. Net loss was $33 million, compared to $15.8 million in profit for the same quarter a year ago.

Chief Financial Officer Yemi Okupe said that revenue excluded $18 million from the “scaling of membership revenue” in the company’s weight loss offering but will be recognized in the fourth quarter.

“This revenue deferral has no impact on free cash flow generation,” Okupe noted.

Adjusted EBITDA was $82.4 million compared to $78.4 million the year prior.

Ethan Feller, stock strategist at Zacks Investment Research, told Fierce Healthcare the company’s revenue was “roughly what Wall Street expected,” adding that U.S. “growth sped up to 21%.”

“But the company lost 14 cents a share against an expected gain of six cents, its third big miss in a row,” Feller said. “It is also keeping less of each sale, as gross margin fell to 57%, down from 74% a year ago, as more of the business shifts to lower-margin brand-name weight-loss drugs.”

Feller added that the company’s “growth story is still a real long-term tailwind.”

“Demand for weight-loss drugs is strong, and having both Novo and Lilly on the platform helps,” Feller said. “But as long as margins keep shrinking, the stock will likely stay under pressure until either the price falls to a level that reflects the lower margins or the company shows it can turn a steady profit.”

As a result, Hims & Hers tightened its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to a range of $3.13 billion to $3.15 billion and reduced its adjusted EBITDA guidance to a range of $257 million to $277 million.

“This is a reflection of the more aggressive strategic pricing and marketing actions that we expect to take in the U.K. and Germany, and the weight loss membership deferral noted above,” Okupe said.

The earnings report comes on the heels of an announcement that the company struck a deal with Eli Lilly to offer its branded obesity treatments directly through the Hims & Hers platform. The drugs were previously only available to patients if they left the site and went to Lilly's direct-to-consumer platform, LillyDirect.

“Nearly 3 million people across four continents rely on us to access care,” Dudum said. “That trust has made us a valuable partner to global pharmaceutical leaders like Novo and Lilly, and positions us to keep bringing the most innovative treatments to our customers as they come to market.”

Dudum added that the company is planning to launch “flexible multi-month subscriptions” across its assortment to make it easier for customers to address health goals.

“We will continue to prioritize partnerships across the industry, with the goal that whenever an innovative therapy reaches the market, our customers can access it here,” Dudum said. “That assortment will sit alongside an AI-native experience that will soon be available to nearly every weight loss customer on our platform.”

#5644. Rheumatoid Arthritis Does Not Improve the Menopause Experience

ORLANDO -- Women with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) had a worse menopause experience compared with the non-RA individuals going through the transition, a researcher reported here.

Symptom severity, as evaluated with the Menopause Rating Scale (MRS), was significantly greater among menopausal RA patients versus other participants in two registries maintained by the Mayo Clinic, with mean scores of 15 as compared with 13 across both cohorts (P<0.001), according to Kristen J. Young, DO, of the Mayo's location in Phoenix.

Moreover, 72% of the RA patients reported a "clinically significant symptom burden," versus 57% in the entire sample (P<0.001), she told attendees at the American College of Rheumatology's annual meeting.

Individual menopausal symptoms including fatigue, sleep disturbance, joint pain, and mood changes appeared worse with RA. Because these are also symptoms of RA, one could also look at these data and conclude that menopause may worsen RA.

In fact, Young did just that. "Menopausal symptoms may compound the existing symptom burden of RA," she said, adding, "Women with RA will benefit" if their rheumatologists take account of menopause.

In discussing the background to the study, Young referenced a British survey of RA patients that included 612 women who were going through menopause, or had done so. Some 80% said their RA symptoms had worsened during menopause. Moreover, Young said, most (93%, according to the original paper) said their rheumatologic care teams never asked at routine visits about how menopause was affecting them.

For the current study, Young and colleagues drew on two datasets compiled at Mayo: the Data Registry on Experiences of Aging, Menopause, and Sexuality, which consisted of women seeking specialized menopause care; and a group of older women receiving broader care called the Hormones and Experiences of Aging cohort. In total, 9,356 women were included in these registries, of whom 215 had RA.

The patient-reported MRS instrument covers three domains: psychological, somatic, and urogenital. The first comprises mood and fatigue; somatic symptoms include hot flashes, sleep, and musculoskeletal complaints; and sexual, bladder, and vaginal symptoms make up the urogenital domain. Eleven questions are posed, with 0-4 points awarded on each for increasing severity. The maximum is therefore 44, but scores that high are vanishingly rare. Total scores of 17 or more are considered severe, and 9-16 is considered moderate. Young and colleagues set 12 as the threshold for a clinically significant burden.

Mean age in the two cohorts was about 54, both for the RA and non-RA participants. More than 90% were white and about 35% had obesity. Roughly 60% were in menopause when completing the MRS, about 10% were perimenopausal, and the rest were postmenopausal. Relatively few were taking hormone therapy. Also, about 500 participants had non-RA autoimmune diseases including lupus, multiple sclerosis, psoriasis, and inflammatory bowel disease.

For the main MRS-based outcomes, the RA group was compared with the entire registry sample that (for reasons Young didn't discuss) included the RA patients as well as those with other autoimmune conditions. Had the RA patients been separated, however, it probably wouldn't have changed the statistics very much, since they accounted for only 2% of the total. And some analyses did compare RA with non-RA participants.

Psychological and urogenital symptom burdens with menopause did not appear worsened at all with RA -- only somatic symptoms seemed to be exacerbated. Total somatic scores averaged 6 in the RA group versus 5 in the total sample. A greater difference was seen when looking at clinically significant burdens in the somatic domain, defined as an MRS score of at least 8. In this comparison, 20% of the total sample had a significant burden, compared with 31% of RA patients.

And joint pain was not solely responsible for this latter difference. Compared with non-RA participants, more of those with RA reported moderate, severe, and very severe hot flashes (49% vs 41%, P=0.024).

Another analysis compared the RA group with participants having other autoimmune conditions on total MRS scores, proportions with clinically significant menopause burdens, and severe hot flashes. Only with RA were these worse than in the total sample, although the smaller numbers of patients with non-RA autoimmune diseases render these differences less reliable. (Interestingly, prevalence of severe hot flashes appeared lower in lupus patients.)

Young noted that the databases didn't include information on RA severity, an important limitation insofar as RA symptoms overlap so much with those of menopause. As well, the study was restricted to women seen at the Mayo Clinic, who may not be representative of either the general population or those with RA.

#5643. Opinion: Low-income parents can’t afford to take chances with nutritious food their picky eaters might reject

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

By Priya Fielding-Singh and Darcy Cherlin

Fielding-Singh is the director of policy and programs at the Global Food Institute at the George Washington University. Cherlin is the research project manager at the Global Food Institute at the George Washington University.

As high food costs and cuts to food assistance squeeze families’ budgets, concerns are growing about whether low-income parents will be able to keep putting food on the table.

But these financial pressures threaten to do more than increase hunger. They also risk harming children’s diets and health in the long run — by making nutritious foods not only harder to afford, but also increasingly risky for parents to buy.

To understand why, consider the most universal of parenting frustrations: picky eating. Most parents experience it, but the stakes vary widely. For well-off parents, watching a child push away a helping of vegetables is annoying but manageable. A carrot left untouched one day can simply mean trying again the next.

But for parents living close to the bone, that same rejected carrot is more than frustrating. It represents money that could have been spent on something their child would have actually eaten.

Simply put: Children’s food refusals come at a cost — one that few cash-strapped families can afford.

Such financial risks profoundly shape how low-income parents feed their kids, as sociologists have documented for years. A decade ago, Caitlin Daniel first showed how the risk of wasting money on rejected nutritious foods led low-income parents to prioritize buying less healthy items they knew their kids would eat. Years later, one of us (Priya) found that catering to kids’ preferences was also driven in part by parents’ earlier bouts of food insecurity: Determined to spare their children those experiences, caregivers often relied on familiar, comforting foods they knew would fill their kids’ stomachs.

Our newest study adds another dimension to this picture. Low-income parents across three states described going to considerable lengths to prioritize children’s nutrition, often at the expense of their own diets.

At the same time, to conserve resources and keep dinnertime from turning into a battle, they paid close attention to their kids’ likes and prioritized buying what they knew their children would eat. As one mother put it, she’d rather her daughter be “happy and fed than sad and hungry.”

Within such severe financial constraints, catering to children’s preferences is strategic. But it can also undermine children’s diets and health over time. That’s because raising kids to be healthy eaters is a long game: Children’s tastes develop gradually as they encounter and become familiar with different foods, and young children often need to try unfamiliar, healthier ones — like bitter vegetables — multiple times before accepting them.

That’s why pediatricians and nutrition experts routinely encourage parents to keep offering fruits and vegetables, even when kids turn them down. It’s smart advice, but it assumes parents can shoulder the costs of following it.

For families with little money to spare, doing so has always been a gamble. And today, it’s becoming an even bigger one. Groceries now cost nearly a third more in dollar terms than they did in 2020. Meanwhile, participation in SNAP — the nation’s largest food assistance program — has fallen by over 5 million people, including an estimated 2 million children, since summer 2025.

These economic pressures are now showing up in parents’ food decisions. A national survey found that more than half of low-income parents reported cutting back on groceries, while over two-thirds worried about having to choose between paying bills and buying healthy food for their children.

Forcing parents into such trade-offs doesn’t just threaten their ability to keep children fed. It also undermines their efforts to help children eat — and learn to enjoy — nutritious foods.

Fortunately, there are ways to address both problems.

First and foremost, we need to ensure children have enough to eat. That means restoring access to food assistance. The next Congress should reverse the cuts to SNAP enacted through H.R. 1 and stop SNAP benefit costs from being shifted to states — a shift that could jeopardize continued access to a program millions of families depend on to put food on the table. To make a bill reversing the cuts veto-proof, it should be a bipartisan effort.

But we also need to invest in programs that support parents’ efforts to feed their children nutritious foods, including incentives that make those purchases more affordable and less financially risky. Protecting and strengthening WIC’s fruit and vegetable benefit and expanding produce incentives like Double Up Food Bucks for SNAP recipients can help families stretch their grocery dollars further, giving them more room to buy nutritious foods their children might not eat the first time around.

Schools and childcare programs must also be critical partners in this work. Beyond providing nutritious meals, they can give kids regular opportunities to encounter and try healthier foods without leaving parents to shoulder the full financial burden. Expanding initiatives like the Department of Agriculture’s Fresh Fruit and Vegetable Program and Farm to School programs, which help introduce children to new foods through fresh produce, taste tests, gardens, and other activities, can help.

Nutrition experts are right to encourage parents to keep introducing healthy foods, even when their children refuse them. But advice that families can’t afford to follow simply won’t cut it. We need food policies that not only ensure children have enough to eat, but also give parents the resources and support to help them develop healthy eating habits that last.

Priya Fielding-Singh is the director of policy and programs at the Global Food Institute at the George Washington University and the author of “How the Other Half Eats: The Untold Story of Food and Inequality in America.” Darcy Cherlin is the research project manager at the Global Food Institute at the George Washington University.

#5642. Scientists discover new Alzheimer’s drug that repairs DNA damage and reduces brain inflammation

Scientists at King's College London have identified a promising new strategy for fighting Alzheimer's disease that could address several of the condition's damaging effects at the same time. Their research suggests that an experimental drug originally developed for spinal cord injuries may help repair damaged DNA, reduce inflammation, and target biological changes associated with the disease.

The drug, known as KCL-286, produced encouraging results in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. Unlike treatments that focus primarily on the buildup of toxic proteins in the brain, this approach targets additional processes that can begin long before the disease reaches its advanced stages.

One particularly promising advantage is that KCL-286 has already completed Phase 1 human safety and tolerability trials as part of its earlier development. This could significantly shorten the path toward further clinical testing, although its effectiveness against Alzheimer's in humans has not yet been established.

"KCL-286 is a first-in-class, orally bioavailable small molecule that has already successfully cleared Phase 1 human safety and tolerability trials. This will dramatically cut down the traditional multi-year timeline required for new drug development," commented Professor Jonathan Corcoran, Professor of Neuroscience at the Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience at King's College London.

The drug is a small molecule that can be taken by mouth, making it potentially more convenient to administer than treatments that require injections or infusions.

Why Alzheimer's Disease Is So Difficult to Treat

Alzheimer's disease involves a complicated series of changes in the brain, making it particularly challenging to develop effective treatments. Two of its best-known features are the abnormal accumulation of proteins called amyloid-beta and tau.

Amyloid-beta can collect into sticky deposits between nerve cells, while abnormal tau proteins can form tangles inside them. These changes interfere with normal brain function and are associated with the progressive loss of neurons, the specialized cells responsible for transmitting information throughout the brain.

Much of the effort to develop Alzheimer's treatments has focused on these two proteins. Although medications that remove amyloid-beta have demonstrated modest but measurable clinical benefits, they do not fully address the many biological processes involved in the disease.

Researchers are increasingly investigating other changes that may contribute to Alzheimer's, including damage to DNA and inflammation in the brain. Both can appear early in the disease process, making them potentially valuable targets for treatments designed to slow its progression.

In the new study, KCL-286 helped repair breaks in DNA and reduce inflammation in mice with Alzheimer's-like disease. These findings suggest that targeting several harmful processes simultaneously could offer a broader approach than focusing on amyloid-beta or tau alone.

"Our findings demonstrate that KCL-286 not only targets DNA damage but also reduces inflammation, two processes that occur very early in Alzheimer's disease progression. This highlights its potential as a disease-modifying therapy rather than simply addressing symptoms," said Dr. Maria Goncalves, who project-managed the drug development.

How Vitamin A Pathways Could Help Fight Alzheimer's

The drug works by activating a particular protein involved in the retinoic acid pathway, a biological system associated with how the body processes and uses vitamin A.

Vitamin A is best known for supporting healthy vision, but it also plays important roles in cellular development, gene regulation, and nervous system function. Retinoic acid, a substance derived from vitamin A, helps control the activity of genes involved in several essential biological processes.

Earlier research found that disruptions in this pathway were associated with the formation of amyloid-beta deposits in the brains of rats. These deposits resemble a major pathological feature of Alzheimer's disease, suggesting that the pathway may be relevant to the condition.

KCL-286 activates a specific protein within this system, offering researchers a way to influence biological processes connected to brain health and cellular repair.

The drug had already demonstrated an ability to promote the repair of DNA double-strand breaks in earlier research involving neuropathic pain, a type of pain caused by damage or dysfunction in the nervous system.

That discovery led scientists to investigate whether the same mechanism might also help address DNA damage associated with Alzheimer's disease.

DNA contains the genetic instructions that cells need to function properly. Although cells have natural systems for repairing damaged DNA, some forms of damage are particularly serious.

One example is a DNA double-strand break, which occurs when both strands of the DNA molecule are severed. These breaks can disrupt normal cellular activity and threaten cell survival if they are not properly repaired.

"DNA double-strand breaks are like a rope snapping completely in two, rather than just fraying at the edges. We found that KCL-286 promotes repair of these breaks, allowing us to target a key feature of Alzheimer's disease," said Professor Corcoran.

The researchers had another reason to suspect that KCL-286 might be useful against Alzheimer's. Previous work by the same team at King's College London identified molecular pathways shared by acute spinal cord injury and Alzheimer's disease.

Because the two conditions involve some overlapping biological mechanisms, the scientists believed that a drug developed to address nervous system damage after spinal cord injury might also improve certain Alzheimer's-related changes in neurons.

Their new findings support that possibility, showing that KCL-286 can influence several cellular pathways involved in the disease.

A Promising New Direction for Alzheimer's Treatment

The results highlight a potentially important shift in Alzheimer's research. Rather than concentrating on one hallmark of the disease, scientists are exploring treatments that address several interconnected causes of brain damage.

KCL-286 is particularly interesting because it targets DNA damage and inflammation, two processes that can emerge early in Alzheimer's progression. Its previous human safety testing also provides a potential advantage over entirely new drug candidates that have not yet entered clinical development.

However, the Alzheimer's findings remain preclinical. Additional studies and human clinical trials will be necessary to determine whether the drug can safely slow disease progression or improve outcomes in patients.

Natasha Hill, one of the first authors on the paper, said: "To develop an effective treatment for Alzheimer's disease, we need to tackle multiple aspects of the disease. KCL-286 was able to target multiple disease-relevant cellular pathways, some of which are initiated very early in the disease course."

#5641. A new tactic in the war over out-of-network bills: Health care providers are suing employers

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Herman examined hundreds of pages of court documents for this story, part of STAT’s Out of Pocket, Out of Reach series.

Bob covers the money in health care, focusing on health insurance and hospitals. His stories delve into Medicare Advantage, opaque prescription drug benefits, and how much executives actually make. He is also the author of the Health Care Inc. newsletter. You can reach Bob on Signal at bobjherman.09.

This past August, Joe Hancock, a Kentucky plumbing and heating contractor, opened a just-delivered box packed with hundreds of sheets of paper. Leafing through them, he read seven words no small business owner wants to see: “A lawsuit has been filed against you.”

The complaint, from air ambulance firm PHI Health, claimed Hancock was on the hook for almost $27,000 in medical helicopter bills. They were tied to one of his now-retired employees, who needed an emergency flight after a heart attack.

Hancock, who owns Whitehead-Hancock Plumbing, Heating & Cooling, a family-run business in Frankfort, Ky., that has been around for more than a century, didn’t understand why he was being roped into a lawsuit that featured 31 other companies — for medical charges he was never aware of.

“I was terrified,” Hancock said. “I was like, ‘What in the hell is going on here?’”

He’s not alone. The PHI lawsuit highlights an evolving tactic by health care providers in a raging battle over out-of-network bills. Previously, providers targeted health insurance companies to pay outstanding amounts that were awarded through federal mediation. Now, they increasingly are dragging the insurers’ clients — employers — into court, claiming they are responsible for bills that insurers haven’t fully paid or have delayed paying. The practice is introducing a new shock that could further torch the affordability of workers’ health coverage.

“These big suits naming dozens of employers at a time is really an escalation,” said Garrett Hohimer, a vice president at the Business Group on Health. “And it will cause employers to incur expenses that [come directly] out of their health care plans.”

A 2022 law called the No Surprises Act shielded patients from the financial trauma of many types of unexpected medical bills, but it has also given rise to a vast industry that’s driving up costs across the health care system. The law uses an arbitration process to determine how much health care providers should get paid for out-of-network emergency care, like helicopter rides, for people who have some type of commercial health coverage. STAT has reported that providers are winning most of these arbitration awards, which often are far higher than the amounts in-network providers receive for the same services.

Already, high payments tied to this process have added approximately $20 billion in extra costs to the health care system, Georgetown University researchers have estimated. A large portion of those costs inevitably come out of the bank accounts of America’s employers and consequently lead to higher premiums, emphasizing how even well-intentioned health reforms can add to the financial pressure that’s crushing workers and businesses.

PHI Health, a national chain, is arguably the most aggressive company suing employers, which it claims are not “passive” bystanders in insurers’ refusal to fully pay awards. Other regional physician practices have sued some employers as well. But PHI and its army of attorneys have filed lawsuits against hundreds of companies, demanding they collectively pay tens of millions of dollars in unpaid out-of-network claims that it won in the federal arbitration process.

PHI isn’t just suing small, local firms like Hancock’s. It’s also taking legal action against some of the largest corporations — Amazon, Walmart, Eli Lilly, United Airlines, General Motors, PepsiCo, State Farm, and Toyota, to name a few — as well as unions, counties, cities, states, public school districts, and universities.

PHI has sued other health care organizations, including hospitals, nursing homes, and medical billing firms. It also has gone after nonprofits, such as the Catholic Diocese of Cleveland. In each instance, a worker or family member at these companies took an emergency medical helicopter, often at a cost of tens of thousands of dollars per trip.

Unpacking the business — and secretive inner workings — of the U.S. health care industry

In some cases, PHI wasn’t sure what company it should be suing, but sued anyway. Several lawsuits named specific health insurers and employers as defendants, and then added “ABC CORP” or “XYZ CORP” as a placeholder. If the insurer or employer “is not in fact the plan sponsor … that covers the patient transported by PHI, then the identity of the plan sponsor is unknown to PHI, and this action is instead brought against ABC CORP,” one lawsuit reads.

Katie Keith and Ellie DeGarmo are attorneys at Georgetown’s Center for Health Policy and the Law who have tracked No Surprises Act lawsuits, including those filed by PHI. They said the scores of cases reinforce the bloat in the health care system: above-market prices that providers are winning for not participating in an insurance company’s network, attempts from insurers to not pay at all or profit off lowball offers, and a booming revenue stream for arbitrators.

But trying to wring money out of employers — and, ultimately, from their workers — is a stark divergence from the public statements of physician groups and air ambulance companies, which have painted health insurers as the bad guys for not following the rules.

“It kind of undercuts the narrative that this is provider versus insurance company,” Keith said. “In this case, this is about provider versus everyone who pays for health care and is now stuck with the bill for [arbitration] awards that have gone totally off the rails.”

STAT reached out to more than two dozen employers that were listed in PHI’s lawsuits. Most did not respond to inquiries. Of those that did, most declined to comment.

“Because this matter involves pending litigation … we will not be providing any interviews,” said Clint Mitchell, the division superintendent of Spotsylvania County Public Schools in Fredericksburg, Va. PHI Health is suing Spotsylvania County’s school system for almost $28,000.

Jay Litten, the town manager of Bridgewater, Va., told STAT the town’s health insurer, Anthem Blue Cross Blue Shield, retained counsel and was handling the case. PHI sued Bridgewater in October for more than $37,000 in unpaid awards.

PHI has boasted about its success in the law’s arbitration process. In 2024, it told prospective investors that it was “able to maintain our profitability” by winning more than three out of every four arbitration claims, and it expected “this trend of favorable” outcomes from the process would continue.

The company has some private equity backing, according to financial filings from when the company considered going public in 2023. Its largest shareholder as of 2023 was Q Investments, a family office that has a private equity firm.

PHI declined to make anyone available for an interview. In a statement, CEO Scott McCarty defended the company’s lawsuits, saying the employers PHI has sued “have a duty to their employees and a responsibility to health care providers in their communities to abide by the law and pay for services delivered.”

McCarty said health insurers are asking their employer clients to choose between paying the unpaid arbitration amounts or authorizing the insurer to continue refusing payment.

“Once an employer is on notice of nonpayment and affirmatively endorses that practice, it is no longer a passive bystander,” McCarty said in the statement. “It has made a conscious decision to allow its insurance company not to pay binding federal awards in violation of federal law.”

In PHI’s lawsuits, the company alleges insurers, and now employers, are using an “unlawful scheme to ‘low pay, late pay, or no pay’ providers, including PHI.” All the cases are still pending.

The company also claims insurers float the money from unpaid awards, which are binding decisions, on the stock market as a way to earn extra interest or investment income.

James Gelfand, CEO of the ERISA Industry Committee, a lobbying group that represents large employers, said companies don’t condone insurers delaying payments as a way to make extra money. But he said under the federal law known as ERISA, employers are legally obligated to make sure they spend their health plan assets wisely on behalf of workers. If employers believe the awards are tied to ineligible claims — or are egregiously high compared with what they normally would pay — those payments could violate that obligation.

As a result, the employers’ health insurers “are operating with our blessing when we say, ‘Hey, if the [arbitration] award is inappropriate and wrong, do not pay it,’” he said. “How can we claim to be responsible stewards of people’s money if we’re just like, ‘Oh, here you go!’ That would be crazy.”

Jenny Goins, who is CEO of the National Alliance of Healthcare Purchaser Coalitions and used to oversee health benefits for Kentucky state employees, said “slow-walking the payments” to providers is one of the only ways employers can push back if they believe the awards are based on ineligible or incomplete claims. Medical claims are not eligible for arbitration if, for example, the employer or its health plan doesn’t cover a certain service or if there is certain information or data missing.

PHI has frequently named Anthem Blue Cross Blue Shield, owned by Elevance Health, as a defendant in the lawsuits against employers. Elevance did not make anyone available for an interview. The company said in a statement that PHI is charging prices for air ambulance services that are 700% of what Medicare pays and mileage rates that are 1,500% more than Medicare rates.

“We have already paid PHI substantial amounts for services provided to our members,” Elevance spokesperson Janey Kiryluik said in a statement. “We dispute whether additional amounts are legally owed for claims that were ineligible” for the arbitration process.

PHI said only arbitrators can determine the eligibility of claims. It added that the rates Medicare pays don’t cover the full cost of emergency air care, nor can those prices be considered during the arbitration process.

The bigger issue revealed by the lawsuits, Goins said, is how “broken” the law has become, even though she believed it was well-intended. The issue has now attracted interest in Congress, where lawmakers are proposing various plans to overhaul the arbitration process.

“Greedy people see an opportunity to make more money,” Goins said. “I also see there’s a true opportunity to shine a light on this.”

In September, PHI dropped Hancock’s company as a defendant, one month after its attorneys served him with court papers. Hancock said his heating, cooling, and plumbing business of 30 employees is not self-insured — meaning he buys his health insurance from Anthem, which takes on all the risk of his employees’ medical care.

PHI’s McCarty blamed Anthem in a statement, saying it “does not always receive clear or consistent information from insurers identifying whether a plan is self-funded or fully insured. In this case, after the lawsuit was filed, Anthem’s counsel confirmed that Whitehead-Hancock was fully insured, and PHI promptly dismissed it, without settlement.”

Other businesses are getting released from PHI’s lawsuits, too. It’s unclear if they were wrongfully lumped in, like Hancock’s company, or if they are paying PHI’s demands to clear a costly legal headache.

PHI’s legal team “threw a handful of darts, and they’re going to try to rattle as many cages as they can,” Hancock said. “It’s not right. It shouldn’t be legal.”

STAT’s coverage of the soaring costs of health insurance for workers and employers is supported by a grant from the Commonwealth Fund. Our financial supporters are not involved in any decisions about our journalism.

#5639. 5 Packing Tips for a Smooth Move

Moving can be a time-consuming process, but it doesn't need to be stressful. We have some tips to help you enjoy a smooth move from your old home to the new. With the right system in place, there is no need to be overwhelmed by the move.

Before you make the move, check out these 5 packing tips.

A common mistake people make when moving is to pack all of their belongings and move them, only to realize upon unpacking that many of the items should have been donated, sold, or thrown out. Before you pack, ruthlessly declutter your home. Packing things only to get rid of them at the new house is a waste of your time and money.

Some questions to ask yourself as you declutter before packing are:

As you pack and move, things are bound to get misplaced. To avoid the stress of a missing document or essential information, keep a folder (either physical, digital, or both) where you won't misplace it that is filled with essential paperwork. This might include:

Greg Dallaire - Green Bay Real Estate Expert says, "Be sure to set up any utilities in the new place to be turned on and ready when you arrive. Even if it means paying for utilities at two places for a brief overlap, it is often worth the convenience. In addition to basics like water and power, call ahead to make sure you will have internet, TV, and any other services you need."

This is also a great time to move additional services to the new address, like security, pest control, or house cleaning.

Even if you are moving all in one day from one Calgary home to another, don't count on being able to unpack everything you need on night one. Instead, pack a suitcase with a few days' worth of clothes and necessities for everyone in the house. This way, you can settle into your new home without scrambling to find a towel or toothbrush before spending your first night there.

The suitcase should include more than just your change of clothes and toiletries. Anything you might need for 2-3 days should be packed in it, including:

As you pack, or have your movers pack, label each box with not just the contents inside but the room it should be placed in at the new home. This way, whether you have professional movers, a team of friends and family, or just your own household, it will be easy to make sure each box lands in the proper place.

One of the easiest ways to do this is by color coding. Assign a color to each room and label accordingly. For example, let's say the kitchen is blue. All boxes that should be brought to the kitchen will be labeled with blue tape, and on move-in day you can hang a large blue paper in the kitchen. This simple system will make unpacking much smoother.

#5638. Scientists discover a surprising clue to autism's origins hidden in the placenta

Scientists are still working to understand why autism develops. Genetics are known to play a major role, but researchers have also found that conditions during pregnancy can influence the likelihood of autism spectrum disorder.

A new study from Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory (CSHL) has uncovered a surprising connection between inflammation during pregnancy, changes in the placenta, and the development of autism-like traits in male mice. The findings suggest that certain developmental disruptions may begin much earlier than previously recognized, potentially offering new clues about autism's origins.

"To truly understand autism spectrum disorder, we have to look beyond the brain," CSHL Associate Professor Lucas Cheadle says. "Our work suggests that maternal immune activation and changes within the placenta are a gateway to autism for some unique individuals."

Scientists Identify an Early Window of Vulnerability

To investigate how inflammation affects fetal development, Cheadle and his colleagues triggered an immune response in pregnant mice at different stages of pregnancy. They used a substance that mimics the immune system's reaction to a viral infection without actually introducing a virus.

The researchers discovered that mouse fetuses were especially vulnerable when inflammation occurred 12.5 days into pregnancy. According to Irene Sanchez Martin, a postdoctoral researcher in Cheadle's laboratory, approximately one-third of the fetuses showed developmental abnormalities within just 24 hours.

Scientists have investigated the effects of maternal immune activation for decades, but these findings reveal signs of developmental disruption earlier than researchers had previously observed.

Even more striking was the difference between male and female fetuses. Across every experiment, autism-like traits appeared only in males, while females continued developing normally.

This unexpected distinction could provide insight into why autism is diagnosed substantially more often in boys than girls. What makes the finding especially intriguing is how early the difference appeared, before many of the biological changes normally associated with sex-specific development.

"It's really fascinating, because we're looking at an age which precedes hormonal surges. It precedes sexual differentiation in the brain and many other regions. So, it's surprising there would be a sex-based difference this early."

A Surprising Connection Between the Placenta and Autism

To determine why some developing mice were affected while others appeared protected, Cheadle and Sanchez Martin examined the placenta, the organ that connects a developing fetus to its mother and supports its growth throughout pregnancy.

Their attention centered on specialized cells called spongiotrophoblasts, which occupy a region of the mouse placenta where maternal and fetal cells interact.

In fetuses that developed normally, this part of the placenta remained healthy. However, male fetuses showing developmental abnormalities also had visible damage to these specialized cells.

Spongiotrophoblasts play an important role in helping the mother's immune system tolerate the developing fetus. This protection is essential because the fetus carries genetic material from both parents and is not genetically identical to the mother.

The researchers found that maternal immune activation could interfere with this protective function. When these placental cells become damaged, the mother's immune response may begin affecting the developing fetus in harmful ways.

Why Female Fetuses May Have a Hidden Advantage

The findings raise another intriguing question: Why were male fetuses vulnerable while females appeared unaffected?

One possibility is that male embryos produce distinctive proteins that can trigger an unfavorable maternal immune response following a viral infection. Another explanation is that female embryos possess some form of protection that helps them withstand inflammation during this sensitive developmental period.

Cheadle says, "A protective mechanism may exist within the female that could be harnessed to help the male. We're trying to understand how autism emerges in both sexes," he explains. "The evidence says that there are potentially different mechanisms."

These possibilities suggest that biological pathways involved in autism-like development may differ between males and females. Understanding those differences could help researchers identify why some individuals are more vulnerable to certain environmental influences during pregnancy.

Cheadle's team plans to investigate both male and female mice more closely to uncover the mechanisms responsible for these contrasting responses. Their work could eventually identify new targets for treatments and lead to strategies for intervening earlier in developmental processes associated with autism.

Although the findings come from experiments in mice and do not establish that the same mechanisms cause autism in humans, they highlight an unexpected possibility: Important clues to autism's earliest development may lie not only in the brain, but also in the placenta and its interactions with the maternal immune system.

#5636. Scientists turn viruses into weapons against deadly superbugs

Viruses are usually associated with causing infections, but some can actually help fight them. Scientists are now working to turn these bacteria-killing viruses into treatments for dangerous infections that no longer respond to conventional antibiotics.

An international team of experts has taken an important step toward making this approach safer and more practical for medical use. Led by the German Society for Infectious Diseases (DGI), the group has developed the first internationally coordinated clinical guidelines for personalized phage therapy, a treatment that uses carefully selected viruses to attack harmful bacteria.

The effort involved 20 professional organizations, 18 international experts, including representatives from regulatory agencies, and two patient advocacy organizations. Together, they established more than 60 recommendations covering how phages should be selected, tested, manufactured, administered, and monitored. The guidelines also address laboratory infrastructure, quality control, treatment documentation, and priorities for future research.

The consensus statement was published in the journal Nature Medicine. Until now, doctors and researchers have lacked a unified international framework for many of the essential procedures and quality standards involved in using phages as medical treatments.

How Bacteria-Killing Viruses Could Fight Antibiotic Resistance

Antibiotic resistance is making bacterial infections increasingly difficult to treat around the world. As some bacteria develop defenses against commonly used medications, doctors may find themselves with few effective options.

One possible alternative involves bacteriophages, commonly called phages. These are viruses that naturally infect bacteria and can destroy them. Unlike many antibiotics, which can act against a broad range of bacteria, phages typically target particular bacterial species or even individual strains.

That precision makes phage therapy especially interesting, but it also creates a challenge. A virus capable of killing one strain of bacteria may have little or no effect on another. Before treatment begins, specialists must therefore determine whether a particular phage can successfully attack the bacteria responsible for a patient's infection.

Personalized phage therapy may be considered when established treatments have failed, are unavailable, or cannot be used safely. Research so far suggests that properly manufactured and administered phages generally have a favorable safety profile. However, controlled clinical trials have not yet provided sufficient evidence to establish how reliably the treatment works.

For that reason, the new guidelines do not recommend phage therapy as a routine treatment for bacterial infections. Instead, they emphasize carefully evaluating individual patients and using the approach only when the circumstances justify it.

Early Results Show Promise Against Difficult Infections

Although major questions remain, early clinical experiences suggest that phage therapy could benefit some patients with difficult infections.

In a Belgian case series involving 100 people who received phage treatment, 77 percent experienced an improvement in their clinical condition. In 61 percent of cases, tests could no longer detect the bacteria that the treatment had targeted.

These findings are encouraging, particularly for infections that are difficult to control with existing medications. However, observational studies cannot establish whether phages were responsible for the improvements or determine how well the treatment would perform in a controlled clinical trial.

Larger, carefully designed studies will be needed to clarify the effectiveness of phage therapy and identify which patients are most likely to benefit.

Finding the Right Virus for Each Bacterial Infection

A central challenge in personalized phage therapy is finding the correct virus for each patient.

Because phages are highly selective, laboratories must test whether a candidate virus can kill the specific bacterial strain involved in an infection. This process, known as a "phage match," should be completed as quickly as possible before treatment begins.

Timing matters because bacteria can change their susceptibility to phages during an infection. If multiple bacterial pathogens are present, specialists should test all of the relevant organisms rather than focusing on just one.

The guidelines recommend that treatment decisions involve a team of specialists, including the patient's physicians, clinical microbiologists, and recognized phage experts. This collaborative approach is intended to help clinicians select appropriate phages and determine whether treatment is justified.

The recommendations also establish expectations for cooperation among laboratories, phage manufacturing facilities, pharmacies, and clinical teams. Consistent testing methods and regular proficiency assessments should help ensure that results from different facilities are reliable and comparable.

Another priority is collecting detailed information about every treatment. The guidelines call for cases to be systematically documented and entered into registries, allowing researchers to compare clinical experiences, identify problems, and investigate unanswered questions.

"The standardization of quality criteria for the production of phages for personalized use, as well as the identification of infrastructural requirements, are essential components of the guideline and important prerequisites for reliable treatments," says Dr. Annika Claßen.

Claßen, a researcher with the German Center for Infection Research (DZIF), played a leading role in developing the recommendations. She also directs the "Translational Bacteriophage Research Group" at University Hospital Cologne.

Other major contributors include PD Dr. Silvia Würstle, Prof. Maria Vehreschild, and Dr. Simone Lieberknecht-Jouy of Goethe University Frankfurt. Vehreschild serves as deputy coordinator of the DZIF research area "Healthcare-Associated Infections," where Claßen, Würstle, and Lieberknecht-Jouy are also involved in research.

German Hospital Begins Using Personalized Phage Therapy

The potential of this approach is already being explored in clinical practice.

"The guideline provides physicians, pharmacists, and regulatory authorities with a common framework for safely and responsibly incorporating phage therapy into clinical practice," says PD Dr. Würstle, the corresponding author of the guideline.

At Frankfurt University Medical Center, Würstle is overseeing the development of the facilities and procedures needed to provide phage therapy in accordance with the new recommendations.

The medical center reports that ten patients have been successfully treated through its guideline-based phage therapy program since February 2026. The treatments use viruses individually selected to target the bacteria causing each patient's infection.

Among the pathogens treated are Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus, two bacterial species associated with infections that can be particularly challenging to manage, especially when antibiotic resistance is involved.

The method of delivering the phages depends on the infection and the patient's medical needs. Treatment may involve intravenous administration, inhalation, a nasal spray, or application through a sterile hydrogel.

These different delivery methods illustrate how personalized phage therapy can be adapted to specific clinical situations rather than relying on a single treatment approach.

New International Standards Could Shape the Future of Phage Therapy

Building a reliable system for phage treatment requires coordination across numerous medical and scientific specialties.

The guidelines highlight PhageNET DZIF, a network established and coordinated by Claßen, as an important platform for exchanging scientific knowledge and clinical experience.

By bringing together expertise in microbiology, clinical medicine, pharmacy, manufacturing, and regulation, the new framework aims to help specialists understand both the possibilities and the limitations of personalized phage therapy.

The recommendations were developed through a structured consensus process under the AWMF (Association of the Scientific Medical Societies in Germany). They are valid from January 5, 2026, through June 29, 2030, with the responsible committee reviewing them annually to determine whether updates are needed.

While phage therapy still requires stronger evidence from controlled clinical trials, these international standards establish a clearer path for its responsible development. For patients facing infections that conventional antibiotics cannot adequately treat, bacteria-killing viruses may eventually provide another valuable option.

The “Breaking Bad” actor is bidding farewell to the property he and his estranged wife bought for $1.7 million in 2024.

According to Page Six, the property first came on the market in September, roughly a year and a half after Bridget filed for divorce in Riverside County.

The property, which is listed with Sherrie Snyder of Allison James Estates & Homes, is described as a "timeless architecturally designed estate with explosive commanding views from one of the most desirable area's of De Luz."

The palatial compound sits on 11.37 acres and totals 7,315 square feet of living space across the main residence and guesthouse.

Together, the two homes have nine bedrooms, seven full bathrooms, and two half-bathrooms. The current asking price is about $1.47 million above what the couple paid.

At roughly 6,067 square feet, the main house contains seven of the estate’s nine bedrooms, with six on the first floor.

Both the living room and the family room boast cozy fireplaces. A third fireplace is in the primary suite, which features exposed ceiling beams and a walk-in closet.

#5633. Goodbye, cavities? Scientists create gel that could regrow tooth enamel

Scientists have developed a new gel that could make it possible to regrow damaged tooth enamel, potentially overcoming one of the biggest limitations in dental care. Unlike bones and many other tissues in the body, tooth enamel cannot naturally regenerate once it has been lost. The new treatment offers a promising way to rebuild this protective layer, strengthen teeth, and help prevent future decay.

The innovation comes from researchers at the University of Nottingham's School of Pharmacy and Department of Chemical and Environmental Engineering. Their new material is inspired by the biological processes that form tooth enamel during early childhood. It is designed to repair enamel that has been weakened by mineral loss or worn away by erosion, while also reinforcing enamel that remains healthy.

The findings, published in Nature Communications, could pave the way for a new generation of dental treatments that go beyond protecting existing enamel and actually help restore its structure.

One of the most promising features of the technology is its simplicity. Dentists could apply the gel directly to teeth using a procedure similar to existing fluoride treatments, making it potentially easy to incorporate into routine dental care.

Unlike conventional fluoride products, however, the new gel contains no fluoride. Instead, it uses a material made from proteins that imitates important characteristics of the natural proteins responsible for guiding enamel formation when teeth first develop.

Once applied, the gel forms a thin but durable coating that penetrates the tooth's surface and fills microscopic cracks and gaps. This coating then provides a framework for rebuilding the mineral structure of enamel.

The process relies on calcium and phosphate ions, two essential mineral components naturally present in saliva. The gel attracts these minerals and helps organize them into new crystals that grow in an orderly pattern.

Scientists call this process epitaxial mineralization. Essentially, it means that new mineral crystals grow in alignment with the existing enamel, allowing the newly formed material to become structurally integrated with the original tooth surface.

This organization is especially important because enamel gets its exceptional hardness and durability from the precise arrangement of its mineral crystals. Simply depositing minerals on a tooth is not enough to recreate the complex structure that makes natural enamel so effective.

By guiding crystal growth, the new gel can restore both the microscopic architecture and the physical properties of healthy enamel.

A Potential Solution for Tooth Sensitivity and Decay

The researchers also discovered that their material can be used on exposed dentine, commonly called dentin in the United States. Dentin is the layer of tooth tissue beneath the enamel. It is softer than enamel and contains tiny channels that can transmit sensations toward the nerves inside the tooth.

When enamel wears away, or gums recede, exposed dentin can make teeth particularly sensitive to hot, cold, sweet, or acidic foods and drinks.

The new gel can encourage the formation of an enamel-like mineral layer over exposed dentin. This could help reduce tooth sensitivity while also improving the attachment of dental restorations, such as fillings and other treatments used to repair damaged teeth.

The potential benefits are significant. Enamel deterioration is a major factor in tooth decay and contributes to dental problems that affect nearly half of the world's population. These conditions can cause pain, infections, and eventually tooth loss. Poor oral health is also associated with broader health problems, including diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

One of the greatest challenges in dentistry is that enamel has no living cells capable of rebuilding it after teeth have fully developed. Although saliva can naturally replace some minerals lost during the earliest stages of enamel damage, the body cannot regenerate substantial amounts of enamel that have been worn away.

Existing treatments, including fluoride varnishes and remineralization products, can help protect teeth and repair early mineral loss. However, they cannot fully reconstruct enamel that has already been lost.

The new technology aims to overcome that limitation by encouraging the formation of new mineral tissue with properties resembling those of the original enamel.

Regenerated Enamel Performs Like Natural Tooth Enamel

The research team tested the mechanical strength and durability of the regenerated material under conditions designed to mimic everyday use.

These experiments examined how the newly formed enamel responded to activities and exposures that teeth routinely experience, including brushing, chewing, and contact with acidic foods.

The results were encouraging. According to the researchers, the regenerated enamel displayed mechanical properties comparable to those of healthy natural enamel, suggesting that the material could provide more than a temporary protective coating.

Dr. Abshar Hasan, a postdoctoral fellow and the study's lead author, explained why recreating enamel's internal structure is so important.

"Dental enamel has a unique structure, which gives enamel its remarkable properties that protect our teeth throughout life against physical, chemical, and thermal insults. When our material is applied to demineralized or eroded enamel, or exposed dentine, the material promotes the growth of crystals in an integrated and organized manner, recovering the architecture of our natural healthy enamel. We have tested the mechanical properties of these regenerated tissues under conditions simulating 'real-life situations' such as tooth brushing, chewing, and exposure to acidic foods, and found that the regenerated enamel behaves just like healthy enamel."

These findings suggest that the gel could eventually offer a way to restore the strength and protective function of damaged enamel rather than simply slowing further deterioration. However, the laboratory results do not yet establish how well the treatment will perform over extended periods in patients.

Beyond its ability to regenerate enamel, the researchers emphasize that the technology was developed with practical dental applications in mind.

The gel is designed to be safe, simple to apply, and suitable for manufacturing on a larger scale. Its versatility could also allow it to be incorporated into several types of dental products, potentially benefiting patients of different ages with enamel erosion, tooth sensitivity, or other problems involving exposed dentin.

Professor Alvaro Mata, Chair in Biomedical Engineering & Biomaterials at the University of Nottingham, led the study and highlighted the potential for translating the discovery into products that dentists can use.

"We are very excited because the technology has been designed with the clinician and patient in mind. It is safe, can be easily and rapidly applied, and it is scalable. Also, the technology is versatile, which opens the opportunity to be translated into multiple types of products to help patients of all ages suffering from a variety of dental problems associated with loss of enamel and exposed dentine. We have started this process with our start-up company Mintech-Bio and hope to have a first product out by next year; this innovation could soon be helping patients worldwide."

The researchers have already begun working toward commercialization through their company, Mintech-Bio, with the goal of introducing an initial product as early as the year following the announcement.

Although further development and clinical validation will be important before the technology becomes an established dental treatment, its ability to recreate the structure and strength of natural enamel represents a promising advance.

If the approach proves successful in patients, it could fundamentally change how dentists address enamel loss, opening the possibility of rebuilding tooth surfaces that previously could only be protected or restored using conventional dental materials.

Materials provided by University of Nottingham. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5630. These Sun Belt States Are Falling Behind on Home Permitting, Study Finds

In an era of strained housing affordability, new-home construction is one of the keys to easing the housing shortage. And some states are building faster than others.

South Carolina, Idaho, and North Carolina lead the nation in permitting new homes, according to data from the Lied Center for Real Estate at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas. On the other hand, the more affordable Midwest was stagnant. UNLV looked at data from the U.S. Census Bureau in the first eight months of this year compared to 2025.

Meanwhile, in the Sun Belt, which has been a bright spot in housing production the past few years, some states are falling behind, a new study finds. UNLV found slowing permitting activity in Texas, Arizona, Utah, and Oklahoma.

"The supply side will determine what housing or rent prices people will face in 18 to 24 months," study co-author Nicholas Irwin said. "And through political action, community members can encourage more development and put pressure on elected leaders to become accountable for rising housing prices."

New permits nationally fell in September—5.2% month over month and 7.4% year over year to an annualized 1.22 million units. Builders in some of these markets are relying on concessions to attract more buyers, but there's no question their confidence is shaken in such a difficult housing market.

For the first nine months of the year, overall new-home sales are 2.9% below where they were in 2025, Realtor.com® senior economist Joel Berner says.

Permits have been the "lone bright spot" in a lot of difficult data, Berner adds.

Housing affordability was top of mind in many swing states this year, and Democrats and Republicans both said they favor reforms that make it easier to build homes. State laws this year could lead to permitting of more homes, especially accessory dwelling units.

UNLV based its study on permits per resident. In total, cities issued 968,187 housing permits nationwide, or abut 2.83 per 1,000 residents. That's essentially flat from the same time in 2025, but it's a 4.1% drop from the same time in 2023.

South Carolina topped the study, permitting 6.07 units per 1,000 residents, a 5% increase from where it was one year ago. Idaho followed at 6.4 units per 1,000 residents, and North Carolina came in third at 5.77 units per 1,000 residents.

Those three states also top a recent Realtor.com report on top new-construction markets.

"These states combine fast-growing economies with favorable new-construction environments to bring homebuyers a larger share of new builds on the market," Berner says.

While Florida, Texas, and Arizona are still in the top 10 states by number of permits, they've slowed the pace of permitting. Rhode Island, New York, and Massachusetts are near the bottom on number of permits, but they've seen notable jumps in how many homes they permit.

Overall, 26 states and the District of Columbia permitted more homes compared to the same time in 2025. The other 24 states permitted less. The biggest drops came in Nevada, whose permit-to-resident ratio is down 29%, and Vermont and Connecticut, which both dropped 18%.

Nevada, which permitted 12,662 units in 2025 and 8,986 this year, joins North Dakota in permitting fewer homes than its projected household growth. That could spell trouble for affordability long-term.

About 64% of the permitted units are single-family, and 3.5% were 2- to 4-unit homes. The remaining 32% of homes are multifamily of 5 or more units.

Much of the housing data this year tells a story of a difficult market for homebuilders, with little relief in sight. This year, Mortgage Bankers Association Chief Economist Mike Fratantoni predicted mortgage rates would remain around 7.3% for the rest of the year and hover above 7% through 2027.

And National Association of Realtors® Chief Economist Lawrence Yun predicted the existing-home sales volume would rise just 4% from last year, having revised that downward this year.

Homebuilders are using incentives to entice buyers, and yet there are more existing homes on the market to compete with newly built ones. Berner explains that's true in the Midwest, often a center of affordability, where demand for homes is softer. Growing cost of land and labor is also making it harder for builders to compete for buyers.

But homebuilders still seeking permits for many units also says something. A permit doesn't mean a home starts construction immediately; it signals future intent.

"Builders are facing diminished buyer demand and high input costs, causing them to slow down when it comes to beginning and finishing projects. But permitting them has held relatively steady," Berner says. "We take this as a sign that builders expect conditions to turn around in the near future, and they want to be ready to capitalize when they do."

The UNLV study points to how affordability has worsened in many areas since 2018, and building new homes is key to improving it.

“Alleviating challenges related to the housing crisis really comes down to a city’s ability to actually build housing," Shawn McCoy, the report's other co-author said. "People need to be able to afford their home, but if they can’t find a home to rent or buy at all, there’s going to be a problem."

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.
