#5614. Credit Scoring Is Changing: 3 Things Homebuyers Should Know

Quick, what credit score do you need to buy a home? If a number pops into your head, there’s a pretty good chance it’s wrong. And the right answer is getting harder to pin down, because the way credit scores are determined and delivered is changing – for the better.

Here’s what you need to know in today’s changing credit climate.

Fannie Mae has been tracking consumer perceptions about mortgage requirements since 2015 and found that consumers consistently overestimated the minimum credit score lenders required to qualify for a mortgage. As recently as 2023, the average guess was 652.

In reality, the long-standing benchmark for loans backed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac is lower, at 620, and today even that isn’t a hard rule for every mortgage they back.

Like the Fannie Mae research, a recent survey from Veterans United found consumers continue to overestimate what it takes to qualify for a home loan:

The takeaway? Guessing wrong can cost you.

A renter who assumes their score is too low and they can’t qualify for a mortgage may never take steps to find out for sure.

For decades, the mortgage industry relied on one set of scores – Classic FICO. Thanks to a push to promote competition, make credit scoring more inclusive, and help more Americans become homeowners, the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) has approved the use of new credit score models such as FICO 10T and VantageScore 4.0.

A different model can mean a different number for the same person. VantageScore says its model can score about 33 million adults that the Classic FICO’s model can’t. So the score you saw on an app last month may not be the one your lender pulls.

Remember: the models may be new, but the basics haven’t changed.

Your credit score is important – no matter how it’s measured. Following the same basic rules will benefit your profile in the old and new score models:

Because while credit models may change, the general advice for you to improve your score doesn’t. Financial awareness and consistency mixed with a little willpower can go a long way.

Don't make credit or homebuying decisions from a chart, an app, or a friend's advice. With the rules shifting and so many misconceptions out there, it's never too early to talk to a professional loan officer for advice on credit, budgeting, and what it would take to qualify for a mortgage.You may be closer to owning a home than you think.

#5613. The Home Insurance Move That Could Save You $440 a Year

When you’re planning a move, every monthly cost counts. That’s why it can be frustrating to see home insurance keep creeping up. According to Intercontinental Exchange, it now makes up 9.6% of the average monthly mortgage payment.

But the latest numbers show some progress on that front – as the increases start to slow down. Here’s what you need to know and what you can do about it.

A look at the past two years shows how much things have cooled down. In mid-2024, home insurance premiums rose 4.3% in a single quarter. By the second quarter of this year, that was down to 1.8%. That’s the smallest quarterly growth in almost 3 years – and that’s a good thing (see graph below):

As Andy Walden, Head of Mortgage and Housing Market Research at Intercontinental Exchange, explains:

“Property insurance has been a fast-growing component of the monthly mortgage payment, but this quarter’s data shows the pace of increase is finally slowing.”

While your premium will likely still go up over time, it may not climb as quickly as it did a couple of years ago. And that’s, at the very least, a step in the right direction.

Here’s where you have some say in what you pay. Let’s take current homeowners as an example. Intercontinental Exchange found that when homeowners shopped around and switched insurance companies, their premiums went down 6.6% on average. Those who stayed with their current company saw an increase of 10.4% (see graph below):

Think about that. That’s a big difference and it goes to show that looking for a new provider can literally pay off.

That works out to about $440 a year in savings for the people who switched. And they didn’t have to give up coverage to get it. Their deductibles dipped 1.4%, and their coverage limits actually rose 7.3%.

While this example is current homeowners, the same general idea applies for first-time buyers too. Shop around and get multiple quotes before you pick your insurance provider. Then, once you’re settled in, review your policy each year when it comes up for renewal. You’re not locked into the first price you get.

The home itself plays a role as well. According to John Burns Research and Consulting (JBREC), newly built homes are 10% to 15% less expensive to insure than older ones nationally.

And while a brand-new home won’t necessarily be the right fit for every buyer, if you’re open to one, it could be one more way to keep your monthly insurance costs down.

Home insurance is certainly a bigger part of the monthly costs than it used to be, and that can feel like just one more thing to juggle when you’re buying a home or moving. But knowing you have ways to keep it in check can take some of the pressure off. Compare a few options before you buy, revisit your policy each year, and lean on trusted local professionals as you plan for your next move.

#5612. Meta introduces Muse Ember to power cost-efficient AI agents

Meta Platforms Inc. today introduced Muse Ember, an entry-level artificial intelligence model that costs significantly less than the competition.

Notably, it’s the first AI that the company trained using Muse Wonder. The latter algorithm is the Facebook parent’s flagship large language model. Meta didn’t specify which part of the workflow it automated with Muse Wonder.

One possibility is that the company used it to perform post-training, the task of honing a model’s capabilities by training it on additional data. Thinking Machines Labs Inc. recently demonstrated that even a relatively small LLM can run post-training runs end-to-end. Anthropic PBC, for its part, last week revealed that its AI models could soon gain the ability to significantly accelerate machine learning research.

Applications often use frontier LLMs such as Muse Wonder as part of AI ensembles. When a user enters a request, the frontier LLM splits it into smaller tasks and assigns them to agents powered by a lower-cost model. Meta says Muse Ember is specifically optimized to play the latter role.

The company evaluated the model using the Artificial Analysis Index, which aggregates nine AI benchmarks spanning use cases such as coding and financial analysis. Meta says that Muse Ember matched the score of Anthropic’s entry-level Claude Haiku 5.5 model at about a third the price. It also outperformed OpenAI Group PBC’s comparable GPT-6 Luna algorithm.

The same internal evaluation saw Meta test Muse Ember and the two rival models across nine other benchmarks. All three algorithms were in “max” mode, which means they used the maximum amount of hardware at their disposal instead of prioritizing cost-efficiency. Muse Ember outperformed Haiku and Luna across seven of the benchmarks.

The area where the model appears to have the biggest edge is business task automation. Whereas most of Muse Ember’s benchmark results were only a few percentage points better than those of Haiku and Luna, it clocked a 17% lead on AutomationBench-AA. It’s a collection of 657 tasks that span popular cloud applications such as Gmail and Salesforce.

Muse Ember has a context window of 1 million tokens, which enables it to ingest lengthy business documents. Users can also include images, audio and video in their prompts. The model generates responses up to 512,000 tokens in length.

Muse Ember is available through Meta’s Model API for 10 cents per million input tokens and 50 cents per million output tokens. A built-in cache can reuse frequently used prompts to avoid duplicate processing. When the feature is active, Muse Ember’s pricing drops to 0.4 cents per million input tokens.

#5611. What Experts Forecast for Mortgage Rates and Home Prices in 2027

When it comes to housing, two of the biggest questions on everyone’s mind right now are:

And if you’re weighing whether to move in the next few months or wait until 2027, here’s what you should know.

When experts look ahead to 2027, they see a steady housing market. No wild swings. No big surprises. Just a calmer, more balanced market.

And steady makes planning a whole lot easier. Let’s break it down.

Lots of people are holding out for lower rates. But the latest forecasts from Fannie Mae, the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), and Wells Fargo show rates holding fairly flat through 2027 (see graph below):

Lenders see it the same way. In a recent survey from HousingWire, 70% of mortgage executives said they expect rates to be around 7.5% or higher six months from now (see graph below):

And if you’re wondering why, the answer is fairly simple. Chen Zhao, Head of Economics Research at Redfin, says:

“Until the underlying economic fundamentals—everything from oil prices to AI–that are keeping rates high change, mortgage rates are unlikely to fall significantly.”

So what does that mean for you? Instead of trying to guess where rates go next, focus on what you can control. Even if rates don’t budge, there are still ways to get the best rate possible. When you talk with your lender, ask about:

Your credit score. Even a small bump in your score could help lower your rate.

Different loan types. Some programs offer lower rates or smaller down payments than you might expect.

Buying down your rate. Paying a little more upfront (called “points”) can lower your rate and your monthly payment.

That way, you’ll know exactly where you stand and what a comfortable monthly payment looks like for you.

But what about prices? Here’s where steady really works in your favor.

Experts don’t see a home price drop coming. On average, forecasts from Fannie Mae, MBA, and Wells Fargo show prices rising about 1% to 1.5% a year through 2027 (see graph below):

In plain terms, in most places prices are still going up, just not as fast. For sellers, that means your home should hold onto its value. For buyers, slower growth gives you a little more breathing room. Just don’t count on prices getting cheaper while you wait.

But keep in mind, these are national forecasts. Prices can look very different from one area to the next, so what matters most is what’s happening where you live.

When the market is steady, you don’t have to try to time it perfectly. There’s no big swing to wait out.

That puts the focus back on you. Maybe you need more space for a growing family. Maybe you’re ready for less upkeep. A steady market makes it easier to plan for either one.

If you’re asking yourself should you move now or wait? You should know experts see a steady market through 2027, with rates holding near today’s levels and prices rising slowly. So, rather than waiting for a big shift that may not come, connect with a local real estate agent and run the numbers on what a move looks like at today’s rates and prices, so you can decide based on your goals instead of the headlines.

#5610. Strategy Buys $82M in Bitcoin as STRC Tokenized Stock Adds New Twist to Saylor’s BTC

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Strategy Bitcoin holdings climbed to 850,364 BTC after Michael Saylor’s company purchased another 1,036 Bitcoin for $81.9 million. The latest acquisition came as Bitcoin traded below the company’s average purchase price, putting its enormous treasury under renewed market pressure.

According to a November 9 SEC filing, Strategy bought the Bitcoin between November 2 and 8 at an average price of $79,012 per coin. Its total acquisition cost now stands at $64.16 billion, with an average purchase price of $75,456.

Strategy has acquired 1,036 $BTC and repurchased $188M of $STRC. As of 11/8/26, we hold 850,364 BTC and $4.9B of USD Assets. $MSTR https://t.co/Pxqso5aVRU

The latest purchase also coincided with a $188.3 million repurchase of Strategy’s STRC preferred shares. The company funded both transactions through its common-stock offering program, highlighting how Michael Saylor continues using capital markets to finance its Bitcoin accumulation.

Strategy sold 2,051,348 shares of its Class A common stock through its at-the-market offering program during the reporting period. The sales generated $283.8 million in net proceeds. The company allocated then $81.9 million toward Bitcoin purchases, while $188.3 million went toward repurchasing 1,887,464 STRC preferred shares. Another $13.6 million was allocated to its general USD cash balance.

The latest transactions show how Strategy accumulation involves more than simply issuing shares and purchasing Bitcoin. The company is also actively managing its preferred securities and liquidity.

Strategy maintained approximately $4.77 billion in its USD Reserve and another $146.2 million in general USD Cash. This reserve supports preferred-stock dividends and interest payments on outstanding debt.

Meanwhile, Bitcoin’s decline below Strategy’s average acquisition price has put its treasury underwater on paper. At $74,000 per BTC, the company’s holdings would carry an unrealized loss exceeding $1 billion. But the latest purchase shows that Saylor has not backed away from accumulation despite the weaker market environment.

The $188.3 million repurchase also puts Strategy’s preferred securities back into the spotlight. STRC, known as Stretch, is a variable-rate perpetual preferred stock designed to trade around its $100 stated amount. It pays cash dividends, with its rate adjusted periodically to encourage price stability.

The instrument has also entered the tokenized securities market through Ondo Finance’s STRCon. Launched in April 2026, STRCon provides blockchain-based economic exposure to Strategy’s Stretch preferred stock. The token is available across Ethereum, Solana, and BNB Chain, subject to geographic and investor restrictions.

Tokenholders receive economic exposure and dividend-related benefits, but do not obtain conventional shareholder voting rights. This gives Strategy’s digital credit securities another distribution channel. Investors outside traditional brokerage platforms can access tokenized exposure through supported blockchain infrastructure.

However, tokenized trading does not generate fresh capital for Strategy automatically. Secondary-market transactions change ownership between investors and do not directly fund additional Bitcoin purchases. Still, this fits into Strategy’s longer-term ambition to build digital credit products for an increasingly tokenized financial system.

Strategy’s latest purchase arrived during a difficult period for institutional Bitcoin demand. US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $1.3 billion in net outflows last week. Last Friday alone accounted for $411.9 million in withdrawals.

BlackRock’s IBIT led Friday’s outflows with approximately $403 million in redemptions. Fidelity’s FBTC recorded $42.8 million in inflows, offering only a partial offset.

Bitcoin also fell toward $74,000 this morning, reaching its weakest level since August. The decline followed broader crypto selling pressure and growing concerns surrounding regulatory uncertainty as AI stocks slide.

The contrast between ETF withdrawals and Strategy’s continued accumulation highlights two different approaches to Bitcoin exposure. ETF investors can reduce exposure through daily redemptions, while Strategy continues using equity financing and its preferred-stock structure to expand its treasury.

Whether that commitment pays off will depend heavily on Bitcoin’s next market cycle, alongside Strategy’s ability to maintain access to capital markets.

#5609. What the Silver Tsunami Means if You’re Planning To Sell

If you’re following the housing market, you may have heard the term “silver tsunami” lately. It’s the idea that millions of homes owned by older Americans could come onto the market as more homeowners reach retirement age and make their next move.

And when you hear a phrase like that, it’s easy to picture a flood of houses hitting the market all at once. But that picture doesn’t match the data.

And if you’re planning to sell, it’s not a reason to put your plans on hold. Let’s look at what the research actually says.

According to Realtor.com, about 13.9 million homes owned by older Americans are expected to change hands by 2036. Sure, that’s a big number. But these homes aren’t all expected to come onto the market at once.

The projections show this happening gradually over the next decade, with roughly 1.3 to 1.5 million homes changing hands each year (see graph below):

Rather than a sudden wave of houses flooding the market, this is a gradual shift as longtime homeowners make decisions about where and how they want to live.

The term silver tsunami makes for a dramatic headline, but the actual data tells a much less dramatic story. And there’s another reason these homes won’t overwhelm the market.

After the 2008 housing crash, builders significantly slowed construction. And for years afterward, they didn’t build enough homes to keep up with demand. That led to a housing shortage we’re still dealing with today.

And just how big a gap are we talking about? Estimates vary, but many experts say the U.S. is still millions of homes short. For example, a recent report from the White House Council of Economic Advisers explains:

“If homebuilding and the growth of the single-family housing stock had continued at their historical pace instead of falling dramatically after 2008, there would be 10 million or more additional single-family homes today.”

As more longtime homeowners sell, those homes will help a gap that’s already there. But they won’t push us over the edge. That’s because, at the same time, more households are expected to form in the decade ahead, and they’ll need homes, too.

So, more homes becoming available over time isn’t automatically a bad thing. It can give buyers more options and help create a more balanced housing market moving forward.

Here’s the takeaway if you’re thinking about selling your house. The silver tsunami isn’t something you need to plan your move around. What’s happening in your local market is far more important than a national projection about the next decade.

That’s because real estate is local. Some markets have more homes for sale than others. Some are seeing houses sell relatively quickly, while others are taking longer.

And those are the conditions that matter when you’re deciding how to price, prepare, and market your house.

For example, an agent who knows your area can help you understand:

How many homes are for sale nearby. This tells you how much choice buyers have and how your house will compare.

What similar houses are actually selling for. That’s one of the most important factors in setting a competitive asking price.

What buyers are looking for right now. Knowing which features and improvements matter most can help your house make a strong first impression.

And that’s something you can act on today, regardless of what happens with the silver tsunami over the next decade.

The right strategy starts with understanding your local market and making decisions based on what’s happening there, not what a dramatic national headline suggests might happen years from now.

The silver tsunami may sound like a major wave of homes coming onto the market, but the research points to a gradual shift over the next decade, not a sudden flood of listings.If you're thinking about selling, don't let that headline make you second-guess your plans. Talk to an agent about what's happening in your local market.

#5608. Inflation Remains Hot in October and Strengthens Case for Another Fed Rate Hike

Inflation accelerated faster than anticipated in October, driven by surging costs for housing and food, which will bolster the case for another Federal Reserve interest rate hike next month.

On a monthly basis, overall prices rose 0.4% from September, according to the Consumer Price Index (CPI) data released by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Tuesday. That's down from the 0.6% monthly increase recorded in September but higher than the 0.2% gain forecasted by economists.

CPI measures the average costs consumers pay for a range of goods, including food, energy, commodities, and services.

Core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy categories, rose 0.3%, also exceeding the anticipated 0.2% gain.

The BLS did not publish an official annual inflation rate because last year's government shutdown prevented the agency from collecting survey data for October 2025.

October saw the index for shelter jump 0.3%, accounting for over 30% of the monthly all-items increase. Meanwhile, the food index increased 0.5%, and the energy index rose 0.7%, coming on the heels of a 5.2% surge in September.

Prices for a wide range of goods and services, including recreation, transportation, medical care, vehicle insurance, education, airfare, and tariff-sensitive categories like furniture and apparel all increased in October.

"These figures hardly qualify as a shock to markets or the outlook, but the details of the report show inflation remains broad-based," says Realtor.com® senior economist Jake Krimmel.

The October CPI print, coupled with the better-than-expected jobs number released last week, signals for the Federal Reserve that it must continue focusing its efforts on combating inflation.

At last month's meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), policymakers voted 10-2 to keep the overnight rate at its current 3.75%-4% range.

However, a December hike now looks all but certain, with odds of a 25-basis-point increase climbing to 99% Tuesday morning, before settling back down to 85%, according to CME FedWatch.

Krimmel says that market reaction is both due to the warmer-than-anticipated CPI print and Fed Gov. Christopher Waller’s latest comments.

Speaking before the inflation report release, Waller put a 50-basis-point move on the table for December and stressed the need to follow through on market expectations for rate increases.

"When this communication is clear and credible, what really matters is that those hikes are eventually carried out," said Waller.

Additional hikes in early 2027 look more in play as well, with the 10-year Treasury going up 9 basis points just 25 minutes after the CPI release.

For housing in the near term, Krimmel says the rising yields and growing speculation about future interest rate increases could put upward pressure on mortgage rates again, reversing a recent downward trend that saw the average rate on 30-year fixed home loans drifting to 7.18% last week.

October’s spike to 7.4% showed how quickly higher rates hurt demand, with contract signings and new listings each falling about 10% from September as buyers and sellers pulled back from the market.

And while rate swings grab the headlines and matter for the marginal buyer, the real wage squeeze is a longer-run, underexplored headwind for demand.

Real average hourly earnings were flat in October as 0.4% wage growth matched 0.4% inflation, leaving annual real wage growth negative for buyers already facing mortgage rates above 7%.

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5607. PitchBook opens its platform to startups for free and debuts Origin deal sourcing service

Private markets data provider PitchBook Data Inc. today opened its platform to startups for free at Web Summit in Lisbon.

Those that sign up have to share their financials. Some of that information will reach investors through the company’s new deal sourcing service, PitchBook Origin.

The launches come as more startups than ever are landing a first round. In the U.S., the 2021 record for first-time financings had already fallen by the end of September, PitchBook and the National Venture Capital Association found in their latest Venture Monitor report.

PitchBook credits artificial intelligence with part of that growth, since the technology has made companies easier to start. AI tools have also compressed investor diligence from weeks to days. Sourcing has not kept pace, the company argues, particularly where the signals are not public.

Free access for startups runs through a program called PitchBook for Startups. Founders who have bootstrapped or raised only from angels, grants or accelerators qualify as long as they are now seeking a first institutional round and can show at least a mockup of their product.

Once a startup has handed over its financials and details on its leadership team and product, its founders can use the PitchBook platform to research which firms are actively writing checks in their sector and stage. Investor research tops PitchBook’s own list of what founders can do with the access.

That founder data lands in a much bigger pool on the Origin side, where coverage starts at about 25 million companies and 250 million people profiles. Bootstrapped businesses and companies that have not yet raised money or announced what they are building are part of that count, and some 15 million of the companies are new to PitchBook.

Third-party data enrichment and PitchBook’s own machine learning models supply part of the coverage. PitchBook said it has not had founder-verified data at scale before.

Each company gets a score, and investors can tune relevance filters to their own criteria. Real-time alerts, saved searches and customer relationship management integrations are meant to replace the manual monitoring that deal teams do now.

Chief Solutions Officer Paul Santarelli said the missing piece for investors has been visibility into “the stage before a company raises, when the most important signals are the hardest to see.” Every company that joins the startup program and contributes verified information sharpens that picture, he said.

PitchBook “was once a startup itself, working to get in front of the right backers,” President and Chief Operating Officer Rod Diefendorf said. Founded in 2007, the Seattle company now serves more than 100,000 clients worldwide. Morningstar Inc. has owned it since 2016.

Startups can apply for the program now. Origin is available as a standalone product or as an add-on to the main PitchBook platform.

#5606. Selling Your Home? What You Should Know About Price Cuts vs. Rate Buydowns.

In today’s market, a growing number of sellers are opting to do something called a price cut – especially when their house has been on the market for a while without any bites.

According to HousingWire Data as many as 4 in 10 (43%) sellers are going this route – that’s the highest it’s been in 4 years. But what if there’s another (potentially better option) for your bottom line? And it’s just as appealing, if not more so, to today’s buyers?

First, let’s set the stage on why some compromise may be necessary in today’s market.

In September, Redfin says there were 63% more sellers than buyers in the market. And with so many sellers active and relatively few buyers by comparison, those purchasers are realizing they have more power. And as mortgage rates continue to put a squeeze on their budgets, they’re leaning in and using it.

One of the most common negotiation points? The price.

That’s because they want to feel like they’re getting a deal and they want to see their monthly payment drop. And since buyers can’t control rates, the price feels like the most obvious lever to pull.

But the savviest sellers realize being flexible doesn’t always mean a lower price, paying for a buyer’s rate buydown might work better.

A buydown is money paid at closing to lower the buyer’s mortgage rate. When you pay it as the seller, you are paying some of the buyer’s interest ahead of time, so the buyer gets a lower rate and monthly payment. And that’s especially appealing to today’s buyers.

Temporary buydowns lower the rate for the first few years, then it goes back to the full rate. The more years a buydown covers, the more it costs. These work well for buyers who expect to refinance within a certain amount of time.

A permanent buydown lowers the rate for the whole loan. These are paid for with “discount points.” One point costs 1% of the loan. According to FICO, each point generally lowers the rate by about a quarter of a percent. This type of buydown works well for buyers who plan to stay in the home for a long time.

And here’s why these can be a win-win for both buyers and sellers. Rate buydowns help sellers stand out in a crowded market and they can have a bigger impact on your buyer than a price cut would.

Here’s an example to show you what that could look like.

Let’s say you’re willing to make a $10,000 concession to help get the deal done. Take a look at these three ways to spend that money and the impact they could have on a buyer’s $420,000, 30-year fixed loan at 7%:

It’s the same $10,000 from the seller. But a 2-1 buydown saves the buyer about eight times more each month in the first year.

And since most buyers shop by monthly payment, that’s what grabs their attention.

That’s what makes a rate buydown worth considering. Instead of reducing your asking price, you may be able to use that same money to have a bigger impact on your buyer’s monthly payments. And depending on what matters most to that buyer, the immediate savings could be more appealing than a price reduction.

The key is working with your agent and the buyer’s lender to compare the options and see which one makes the most sense.

Loan programs cap how much a seller can pay toward a buyer’s costs.

Money toward buydowns doesn’t limit what else a buyer may ask a seller to pay for. Buyers may still ask for repairs or other concessions.

Putting the buydown offer in your listing lets agents and buyers know it’s an option.

Your agent can run scenarios on buydowns and other costs of selling in advance so you’re prepared when an offer comes in.

As Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), says:

“Home sellers need to be realistic about local market conditions, which could require price discounts and other incentives to attract buyers.”

And sellers who offer solutions like buydowns can make meaningful impact where home buyers need it most: in their wallets.

When you're looking for ways to make your house more appealing to buyers, a price reduction isn't your only option. A mortgage rate buydown could help a buyer save more each month, especially in the early years of their loan.Talk to your agent or a trusted lender which incentives could make the biggest difference for buyers in our market, while still protecting your bottom line.

#5605. Reality Star and Real Estate Tycoon Ryan Serhant Expands Brokerage to Utah

Real estate mogul and star of Netflix show “Owning Manhattan” Ryan Serhant is launching his rapidly expanding brokerage in another major metro, marking his sixth new state in 2026.

The national brokerage, SERHANT., announced its expansion into Utah on Tuesday, bringing its team of top agents and proprietary AI platform to Salt Lake City and Park City.

The new market is the latest of several victories for the brokerage this year, which has expanded into Massachusetts, California, Texas, Colorado, and Illinois in 2026 alone.

With the addition of Utah, SERHANT. is operating in 21 states.

“There’s an established luxury market in Salt Lake City and Park City, which is in line with what we do,” Serhant tells Realtor.com®. “It’s a natural connection point for the business that we’ve been building nationally because a prospective buyer in this marketplace is oftentimes already a client of ours in New York, Miami, Dallas, L.A., etc., so we can bring those relationships together.”

Salt Lake City is among the fastest growing cities in the country, with the downtown population increasing 63% since 2019, according to the Downtown SLC Alliance. As the area continues to develop and grow, an opportunity presents itself to entrepreneurs like Serhant.

“Utah will be one of our larger individual market launches, considering that Park City alone did about $5 billion in residential sales over the past 12 months,” says Serhant. “So it’s a good market to go in. I’m excited to bring SERHANT. there and work with as many buyers, sellers, developers, and agents as we can.”

SERHANT. Utah will launch with over 40 agents from top firms, who together have closed $700 million in sales over the past 12 months, according to a press release from the company.

“We’ve been very fortunate that the types of agents who’ve come to us, who are looking to either be founders in our new markets or grow with us in existing markets, are really the best of the best,” Serhant says.

Agents looking to join SERHANT. must meet high thresholds: Agents must do at least $10 million per year in sales, while principal agents must hit $50 million per year. Such qualified agents are essential in a market as demanding as the Utah luxury market, according to Serhant.

“A more demanding market raises the standard for everyone because sellers need strategy outside of the box to work with a firm that creates markets; it doesn’t just put homes on top of it. Buyers need real advice—trust cannot be automated,” says Serhant. “And agents need a company that helps them win business and grows their own market share and price point so that they can serve their clients better. And all three of those boxes are what we check."

The team in Utah will be led by managing director and principal broker Bridgette Osguthorpe, a leader in Utah’s luxury real estate market with more than 20 years of experience.

“When I looked at what SERHANT. has built, nothing else compared,” said Osguthorpe in the press release. “The tools and resources they give agents for their day-to-day business are best in class, and they pair that with genuine care for and connection with their people. That combination sets SERHANT. apart.”

Park City-based agent  Julie Snyder will join SERHANT. Utah as a Founding Member, bringing more than $350 million in career sales and a deep care of the state’s natural resources.

“Becoming a Founder at SERHANT. Utah was about finding a company that better matches the way I think about real estate,” said Snyder in the press release. “SERHANT. has built a company around marketing, media, technology, creativity, and innovation in a way that feels aligned with where this industry is headed.”

In addition to working with some of the top names in Utah Real estate, Serhant and his company have developed a proprietary AI platform, S.MPLE, which provides every agent with a powerful generation, marketing, and transaction management tool. With the use of S.MPLE, agents can save hours per week on administrative tasks and focus on providing the best quality service o the best quality properties.

“It saves agents money on administrative tasks and help that they’d otherwise be needing to spend. It helps increase sales volumes: Our average agent who uses it grows their transactions by 44% in the first year,” says Serhant. “It’s totally changed the game—and within a context window and compliance guardrails.”

Due to Serhant’s own impressive sales record of over $10 billion in lifetime sales and his successful Netflix show garnering extensive attention, SERHANT. has more than 11 million followers across social media channels, making it the most followed real estate brand in the world. This creates an organic flow that helps both the company and prospective clients, according to Serhant.

“We reached our clients in the palm of their hand before they ever see an ad,” says Serhant. “It’s an organic distribution funnel for real estate: hyper-specific, across language, across demographic, and across geographic regions to drive organic lead flow for people who are looking to buy, people who are looking to sell, and people who are looking to develop.”

#5604. AI security startup Bay launches with $50M to vet agent actions before they run

Israeli artificial intelligence security startup Bay AI Inc. launched today with $50 million in funding to let enterprises vet each action an AI agent tries to take before it runs.

Bay provides software that tracks the agents working across a company, whether they sit on an employee’s laptop, inside a cloud workload or in a software-as-a-service application. One set of policies covers them all.

First-generation AI security tools mostly filter prompts and responses. Bay argues that misses where the damage happens, since a harmless-looking prompt can still end with an agent deleting a production database.

The founders ran into that kind of failure themselves when one of their own coding agents, working with its normal permissions, tried to expose a cloud environment to the internet to finish a test. They still have the screenshot.

Bay installs through the mobile device management or endpoint detection and response tools a customer already has, and the company says it takes under five minutes. A scanner called Wave inventories the agents, extensions and local models on each machine and leaves nothing running once it finishes.

Each time an agent proposes an action, the AI tool running it hands the request to Bay Enforcer, a static binary, through a native hook. The check happens on the machine itself with the whole session as context, and Bay said a verdict comes back in milliseconds, sometimes as a prompt asking the user to approve the step. Anything judged too risky never runs.

The policy behind those verdicts comes from Bay’s Lighthouse system, which drafts a separate one for each team from the last 30 days of agent activity, so security staff are not writing rules every time someone picks up a new tool. Teams can test a policy against the previous month first and see what it would have stopped. Bay said false positives run under 1%.

Security leaders are often handed an enterprise-wide AI rollout with a year-end deadline, co-founder and Chief Executive Yuval Zacharia said, or find that agents have already spread across the company and “it’s the Wild West.” She wants security to become “the reason AI ships faster, not the reason it stalls.”

Micron Technology Inc., Wix.com Ltd., ClickUp Inc. and Peloton Interactive Inc. are among the dozens of enterprise customers signed in the nine months since Bay was founded. Fortune 100 companies on the platform tripled their use of autonomous agents in just under 30 days, the company said.

Zacharia founded Bay with Chief Product Officer Aner Morag and Vice President of Research and Development Boris Danilovich. The three knew each other from the Israel Defense Forces’ Unit 8200, where Zacharia led a department of about 50 people before becoming the first intelligence officer there to cross into offensive cyber operations. After the military she ran security research and AI at Cyber Hunters Ltd.

Danilovich was an early employee at Preempt Security Inc. and stayed six years at CrowdStrike Holdings Inc. after it bought the startup in 2020. Most of Bay’s research team followed him over. Morag was the first employee at Noname Security.

The $50 million comes from two rounds. Battery Ventures LP led the larger $37 million Series A round, and Micron’s venture arm, Micron Ventures, also participated after the chipmaker started out as a Bay customer. Wiz Inc. Chief Executive Assaf Rappaport put in money personally. The remaining $13 million came from a previously undisclosed seed round co-led by YL Ventures Ltd. and Striker Venture Partners.

Yoav Leitersdorf, managing partner at YL Ventures, said his firm looked at a crowded field of AI endpoint security companies before picking Bay. He believes it can become “as fundamental to enterprise AI adoption as the network firewall was to the internet era.”

Engineering and product hiring will continue in Tel Aviv, where Bay is based, with the sales, marketing and customer teams growing in the U.S. and Europe. Enterprises can buy the platform now.

#5603. Johnson Development’s Jubilee Earns the First WELL Residence Certifications in Texas

The International Well Building Institute (IWBI) has recently awarded 185 homes in Jubilee a WELL Residence certification. The 1,622-acre community by Johnson Development is the first in Texas to have homes receive the certification.

Signifying they have met a global standard for healthier, more resilient homes, the 185 residences represent 478,493 square feet of development and is the second group of Jubilee homes to receive WELL certification, with 125 homes earning the designation last year.

“We’re always excited about these certifications because they provide third-party recognition that we are actually building a community that truly prioritizes wellness and isn’t simply a marketing pitch,” said Nick Deacon, Jubilee Development manager. “Having the respected independent IWBI validate our efforts makes the achievement that much more meaningful.”

Up from the minimum 40 criteria used to certify homes last year, the homes met 45 criteria to earn their certifications. Categories considered span from air and water quality to light, sound, and thermal comfort.

Deacon added, “It’s encouraging to see us continuing to build on what we learned from our first submission.” Another 215 homes have been submitted for certification with the goal to have all homes in Jubilee earn the WELL Residence seal.

Jubilee was the first Texas community to become an early adopter of IWBI’s WELL for residential program in 2023. Today, 4,470 units around the world representing 6,820,597 square feet have received a WELL Residence certification, according to IBWI. Johnson Development was one of 25 early adopters across 10 countries.

Every home in Jubilee is built with a variety of wellness features, including a reverse-osmosis filtration system at the kitchen sink; a fresh-air intake and a MERV 13 media filter; circadian rhythm lighting for the family room, kitchen, and primary bedroom; and a central automation system.

“Your home—your community—should be your sanctuary,” Deacon said. “Jubilee is designed to be just that, a place where you can rejuvenate, relax, and take comfort.”

Builders include Beazer Homes, Chesmar, Coventry Homes, David Weekley Homes, Highland Homes, J. Patrick Homes, Newmark Homes, Perry Homes, Tri Pointe Homes, and Westin Homes.

#5602. Inside Josh Allen and Hailee Steinfeld’s Multimillion-Dollar Real Estate Portfolio

Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen's football career continues to go from strength to strength, with him most recently leading the New York-based team to victory against the Minnesota Vikings.

The 30-year-old athlete, who has been with the Bills since being selected in the first round of the 2018 NFL Draft, previously added an overtime win to his resume, marking a significant personal achievement for the football star.

Now, he has once again showed off his skills in the Bills vs Vikings game, which saw the Bills leading 23-6 on Nov. 9.

The victory is another highlight in Allen's impressive career, which has seen him become one of the NFL's most recognizable quarterbacks.

However, while Allen continues to make headlines for his accomplishments on the field, his life away from football is equally impressive—particularly when it comes to the multimillion-dollar real estate portfolio he shares with his actress wife, Hailee Steinfeld.

Allen and Steinfeld, 29, tied the knot on May 31, 2025, during a romantic ceremony at San Ysidro Ranch in Montecito, CA, nearly two years after their relationship first became public.

The couple welcomed their first child, a baby girl, in April 2026, adding another milestone to what has already been an eventful period in their personal lives.

Although Allen, who was born in Firebaugh, CA, spends the majority of the season in Buffalo, he has maintained a close connection to the Golden State, snapping up a $7.2 million property in Dana Point back in 2023.

The four-bedroom, three-bathroom dwelling is located inside a "prestigious" guard-gated community that features its own private beach club—and offers proximity to a host of nearby five-star resorts, including the Ritz Carlton.

It's understood that Allen spends much of the offseason at his California abode, soaking up the warm weather after a traditionally frosty Buffalo winter.

However, the sporting sensation also boasts another very sizable dwelling much closer to the Buffalo Bills' training ground and stadium: a custom-built megamansion that he had erected on a plot of land he snapped up in 2021 for the relatively low price of $500,000.

Records show that he purchased the 31-acre plot via an LLC, with Google Maps indicating that he has had quite the impressive property built on it.

Located in the tony community of Orchard Park, approximately eight minutes away from Highmark Stadium, the home features a stunning swimming pool, pool house, and a private sports court that can be used for both basketball and tennis.

Additionally, there is a private lake on the land, which has been outfitted with a small dock as well as a waterfront seating area that can be accessed via steps that lead down to the water from the pool.

Ironically, the property appears tailor-made for summertime activities, despite the fact that the football season takes place largely during the colder months.

Still, it provides the perfect place for Allen to lap up the last of the warm weather when he returns to Buffalo for preseason training camp, which kicks off on July 24.

However, thanks to his fiancée, the NFL pro also has his pick of properties over on the West Coast—where Steinfeld also owns a dazzling abode, which she picked up for $8 million back in 2021.

Located in Encino, CA, more than an hour away from Allen's Dana Point dwelling, the home was previously owned by rocker John Fogerty, who sold it to Steinfeld for $7.98 million—more than $3 million more than he had paid for it in 2018.

The actress' property spans an impressive 9,000 square feet and features six bedrooms and eight bathrooms. Much like her beau's abode in Buffalo, it has a sizable private pool, which can be accessed via a motorized window wall that opens up from the main living area into the backyard.

Upstairs, the primary suite features its own sitting room as well as two fireplaces, two walk-in closets, and two bathrooms—perfect for the couple that prefers to have their own space to get ready in the morning.

Cozy date nights can be enjoyed in the home's private movie theater, while the couple can host plenty of guests in the property's lounge, bar, or great room that has a custom "floor-to-ceiling entertainment wall."

And while the backyard has ample space for entertaining—and even includes an outdoor kitchen—that is not the only place where the pair can kick back and enjoy the open air.

In addition to the yard, there is also a roof deck on the property, which provides an additional outdoor space for relaxation or sunbathing.

However, if the pair are hoping to invest in property together, they may look elsewhere in California, specifically Malibu, which is where Allen popped the question to Steinfeld on Nov. 22, 2024.

The actress opened up about the proposal during a February interview with Who What Wear, telling the publication that Malibu serves as her "happy place" and adding that she couldn't have been happier with how the proposal happened.

"I'm so grateful that he did it the way he did so that I looked good, and we have these photos that we'll have and cherish for the rest of our lives that I'm not looking at being like, 'What was I wearing?'" she said. "We were in Malibu, which is my happy place, and it was magical."

"When you realize that so much is already out there in every other aspect of your life, you really learn to cherish the little that isn't. It just makes things extra special, and it's just for you," she explained.

#5601. The 2027 Paint Colors of the Year Take an Emotional Turn

In the past, one hue typically dominated paint colors of the year, with different brands interpreting the color. For 2027, while there are a few blues and greens on offer, there is a much wider variety. Themes are less color-specific and more about emotional intent.

“Color has always been tied to emotion. We instinctively use it to create spaces that make us feel a certain way, and the colors we choose often reflect what we’re looking for in our lives,” says Lisbeth Parada, color marketing manager for Dutch Boy and Minwax brands.

​In 2027, that’s digital detox, permission to be authentic, and the opportunity for stillness and reflection.

​“We’re living in a world increasingly shaped by technology, algorithms, and an almost constant stream of information telling us what to think, what to buy, and how to live. We sense a growing desire to reconnect with our own instincts and the tangible experiences that make us feel human,” says Phillipa Radon, interior designer and C2 paint color specialist.

This year’s color trends tell us it’s not enough to treat home as a retreat anymore; recharging is necessary too, to manage the fast pace of the world around us. The variety of colors suggests multiple ways to gather that energy, with consumers choosing what resonates with them.

In new-construction homes, color choice is even more important, with paint offering homeowners a powerful way to personalize a brand-new space and forge that emotional connection to restoration.

​Here are the paint colors of the year for 2027.

​Sometimes paint color names are intentionally vague as part of their marketing micro-story. Not BEHR’s Grounded, with a name and a mossy green color that instantly frame the experience.

Its name has a double meaning too, as an invitation to breathe and get back to basics, amid digital overwhelm.

“What makes Grounded so relevant as BEHR’s 2027 Color of the Year is the way it balances two things people increasingly want from their homes: calm, and a feeling of life,” says Kayla Kratz, head of color at BEHR.

She notes that for many years, that meant paring down to a minimalist aesthetic, but today’s homeowners want more warmth and personality.

“Grounded answers that shift. The moss and olive tones bring a natural vitality, while warm brown undertones add depth and steadiness. The result is restorative without being static.”

Kratz says that the color replicates the dynamic greens of a forest, evolving throughout the day and changing light conditions.

​Deep Rooted, a nature-inspired warm orange, is energetic but steady and reassuring.

​“There’s an optimistic quality to the color. It has enough richness and energy to support bold contrasts and individual expression. The name brings those ideas together: feeling rooted while remaining open to possibility, and Deep Rooted captures that balance,” says Parada.

​It’s a perfect example of how paint color names are shaping the experience this year, with this color meant to encourage strength by standing still, not always easily done in today’s fast pace of living.

“​The paint color name captures both the color’s connection to nature and the sense of grounding many people want their homes to provide. At home, that translates into spaces that feel personal, welcoming, and comfortably lived in,” says Parada.

​Artifact is a smoky, atmospheric blue intended to create space to pause, recalibrate, and think more clearly after you’ve had a chance to catch your breath. These moments in time are both treasured and rare, which is reflected in the paint color name.

Artifact also embraces the idea of authorship, and how major change doesn’t necessarily require a makeover.

​“As consumers move away from creating homes that look like everyone else’s, they’re focusing on spaces that reflect who they are, where they’ve been, and what matters most to them, “ says Ashley McCollum, color marketing manager at Glidden.

​“People don’t necessarily want to reinvent themselves or start from scratch but rather make thoughtful adjustments that help their life feel more balanced and manageable,” says McCollum.

​“Artifact is not a reinvention, but a readjustment. It brings a sense of ease and relaxation after a busy day, helping you to unwind and feel more grounded. As a mid-tone, smoky blue, it leans warmer and has depth that strikes a balance between focus and comfort.”

This calming blue is nuanced and versatile, the kind of color that’s felt before it is seen, making it a good choice for homeowners who are choosing colors for an emotional impact.

Celery is a light green with yellow undertones that feels more herbal than botanical. It’s fresh and lively, marking a transition for Sherwin-Williams’ color trends.

Their paint color of the year last year was Universal Khaki, inspired by nostalgia and the comfort found in familiarity. Celery takes that feel-good energy into the future on a positive note. The color emerges alongside consumers’ appetite for expressive colors and a continued focus on wellness design.

A few paint colors of the year for 2027 are green, a carryover from last year’s color trends, but Celery offers a different perspective.

“While deeper, earthier greens have helped create grounded, restorative spaces, we’re beginning to see that nature-inspired palette evolve in a more expressive and optimistic direction,” says Ashley Banbury, color market manager at Sherwin-Williams.

“Celery reflects this shift, bringing a lighter, more playful energy to a color family that homeowners already know and love. It shows that green can be both calming and invigorating, offering a fresh perspective on nature-inspired design while encouraging homeowners to embrace color in more personal and unexpected ways,” says Banbury.

C2’s Pueblo is one of the more dynamic colors this year, with its identity shaped by an intentional refusal to commit to a single hue.

“What makes Pueblo so fascinating is that it resists a single definition. At its heart, it’s a warm, muted rose that bridges the space between deep floral tones and earthy neutrals. Its nuanced undertones interact with the changing temperature and intensity of natural light, revealing different aspects of the color throughout the day,” says Radon.

​“That complexity brings an unusual sense of dimension to an interior. Rather than creating a static backdrop, Pueblo becomes part of the experience of living in a space.”

​In the context of this year’s color themes, Pueblo taps into the idea that creativity and movement create energy to digitally detox.

​“There’s a certain confidence in choosing a color like that. It suggests we’re ready to move beyond simply creating a sanctuary and begin using our homes as places for creativity, individuality, and renewed engagement with life,” Radon says.

​Benjamin Moore has gone all-in on timeless over trends this year with their choice of Webster Green, a classic forest green that the paint brand is betting has staying power, given how prevalent various shades of green have been in color trends over the last few years.

​Green is adaptable and inherently energizing, which makes this shade a relevant tool for homeowners who want something sturdy but stylish too. Timeless design and decor choices are becoming more important to homeowners, for the sake of affordability and sustainability too.

​“Webster Green reflects this timeless appeal by pairing reassuring stability with optimistic energy. Its composed nature feels both rooted and forward-looking, while enhancing spaces that feel distinctive, collected, and continually new,” says Andrea Magno, vice president of brand, color, and integrated marketing, at Benjamin Moore.​

​A sultry brown with plum undertones, French Press Coffee is all about striking the right mood and elevating daily rituals, another approach to gathering energy ahead of the daily grind. It’s the color equivalent to providing time and space to savor a hot, highly flavorful cup of coffee.

​It’s a little more nuanced than some of the other moody hues released in years prior, thanks to multidimensional color that adds visual weight and interest, while broadening potential applications.

​”French Press Coffee is the kind of color that reveals itself gradually,” said Lauren Hoferkamp, color marketing manager at Dunn-Edwards. “As light shifts throughout the day, its subtle plum undertone emerges, adding complexity you don’t always see in a neutral. It’s grounding and restrained yet full of character.”

Blues dominated 2023’s colors of the year for their spa-inspired calm, and Valspar is rekindling those vibes. Chosen for being familiar but fresh, Cottage Door is a mid-toned blue with warm undertones.

Sue Kim, director of color marketing at Valspar, says that the color, “is reflective and warm, with timeless appeal that feels personal and grounding. Cottage Door captures blue’s natural sense of security and trust while serving as a colorful new neutral that layers effortlessly into the home. It creates spaces that feel balanced, comforting, and inviting.”

The color taps into consumers’ increasingly pragmatic view on home design, and the company touts it as “designed for real life.” Homeowners would rather choose a color that endures than redecorate tomorrow.

This article was originally published on NewHomeSource.com.

Heather Wright is a senior writer for NewHomeSource and Builder with a background in real estate reporting and home design, decor, and architecture. She has written for a number of print and digital publications in the lifestyle space.

#5600. Teleport makes Beams generally available to bring AI agents into production

Infrastructure identity company Teleport today made Teleport Beams, its runtime for artificial intelligence agents that work on production infrastructure, generally available.

Beams goes after what Teleport sees as the main reason agents have stayed out of production so far. Most enterprises have not plugged agents into those systems at all, according to Ev Kontsevoy, Teleport’s co-founder and chief executive. He blamed gaps such as delegated identity and an audit trail that follows an agent from intent to action.

Sandboxes, the tool many teams reach for now, mostly isolate the agent in a virtual machine and handle its credentials. “When the cost of an error is high, traditional sandboxes don’t cut it,” Kontsevoy said ahead of the announcement.

Teleport calls each individual runtime a Beam, and every agent gets its own. A Beam carries a delegated identity inherited from the user or agent that launched it, while the agent inside starts with no standing privileges. Work begins with a proposed execution plan. That plan can be revised by a person or by a large language model acting as judge before a separate Beam runs it with only the approved roles. Reviewers then see new requests only for steps outside the plan.

Passwords never enter the agent’s environment. Everything the agent sends to a model is traced, and Teleport says that record lets Beams pick out a hijacked goal or agents coordinating in ways nobody planned. Each session also gets scored against the MITRE ATT&CK framework for a written risk summary. Seven of the detection rules come prebuilt, privilege escalation among them. Anything else a customer wants caught can be described in natural language and added to the set.

Each Beam is an ephemeral micro-VM on a virtualized network. Nothing gets in or out without passing Teleport’s controls, and the audit log keeps a copy of every protocol exchange. Snapshots taken by a feature named Phases carry the files and memory of an expiring Beam into the next one, so longer jobs do not have to start over.

Teams can also fork a Beam to try several approaches in parallel. When something goes badly wrong, a kill switch ends the agent’s activity and cuts all of its connections to production at once.

Teleport makes no promise about what a model will decide. A hijacked or mistaken agent inside a Beam can reach only what it was granted until its authority lapses at the end of the task, and every action it takes stays on the record.

Beams runs on top of the Teleport Infrastructure Identity Platform, which the company says is in production at more than 700 enterprises, Nasdaq Inc., DoorDash Inc. and Elastic N.V. among them. Cisco Systems Inc. became Teleport’s largest strategic investor in August.

Teleport first showed Beams in March, two months after publishing the Teleport Agentic Identity Framework that the runtime now puts into practice. Following a public beta, the product is available at beams.run.

#5599. How Traton Homes Is Designing for Multigenerational Living

The Presley model's guest suite at The Tillery in Marietta, Georgia.

Today’s buyers are asking their homes to work harder over time. At Traton Homes, main-level guest suites have become an important part of that flexibility, providing space for overnight visitors today and potentially aging parents, caregivers, or other family members in the future.

Director of design Angi Sago explains how evolving household needs are influencing the builder’s approach to floor plans, entertaining spaces, and long-term livability.

Traton offers a variety of floor plans featuring a guest suite on the main. What does that tell you about how buyer priorities are changing?

Buyers are increasingly looking for homes that offer flexibility to accommodate their families’ changing needs. A private guest suite on the main level provides a comfortable space for visiting family and friends, but it also offers the opportunity to accommodate aging parents, whether for extended visits or as a more permanent living arrangement in the future. It’s a feature that adds both immediate convenience and long-term value.

Who are these suites designed for; aging parents, adult children, long-term guests, or a combination?

The Presley model home at The Tillery in Marietta, Georgia.

While these suites certainly provide a wonderful space for overnight guests, we find that many buyers are thinking about aging parents and the possibility of multigenerational living. Having a private guest bedroom with en-suite bath on the main level gives homeowners peace of mind knowing they have a comfortable and accessible space for loved ones, whether they are visiting or eventually become part of the household.

How has demand for multigenerational or guest-friendly living influenced Traton’s floor plans over the past few years?

Traton has recognized the appeal of main-level guest suites for many years, and we’ve incorporated them into our home designs for quite some time. These floor plans have consistently been popular because they offer homeowners flexibility in how they use their space. As families’ needs continue to evolve, we believe this versatility is becoming even more valuable to today’s buyers.

What separates a well-designed guest suite from simply putting an extra bedroom and bathroom on the first floor?

Are buyers looking for spaces that can change purpose over time, such as moving from a guest suite to an aging-in-place bedroom or caregiver space?

Absolutely. Flexibility is one of the greatest advantages of a main-level guest suite. A space that initially serves as a bedroom for visiting friends and family can eventually accommodate an aging parent or caregiver. Buyers appreciate knowing their home can adapt to different stages of life without requiring significant changes to the floor plan.

Beyond the guest suite, what design features are becoming more important for homeowners who regularly entertain or host overnight visitors?

Spaces that make entertaining easier and more enjoyable continue to be popular. Butler’s pantries are especially appealing because they can double as a beverage or bar area while providing additional storage and serving space. Keeping rooms are another desirable feature, offering a comfortable, informal gathering area where family and friends can relax and spend time together. Buyers appreciate having spaces that encourage connection while allowing for different types of entertaining.

The Abney model at Linden Grove in Powder Springs, Georgia.

Traton’s floor plans with owner’s suites are offered at various price points. How do expectations for hosting and flexible living differ between by price point, if at all?

Interestingly, we see many of the same priorities across price points. Regardless of price point, homeowners want comfortable, functional spaces where they can welcome family and friends. The primary difference is often the amount of space available for entertaining and the additional features a larger home can accommodate. While buyers of our more expansive homes may have more gathering areas, the desire for a private guest suite and flexible living spaces is equally important to buyers of our more moderately sized plans.

Are buyers willing to give up square footage elsewhere in the home to get a main-level guest suite, larger pantry, loft, or other flexible space?

We find that a main-level guest suite is typically a feature buyers either prioritize from the beginning or don’t necessarily need. Rather than sacrificing square footage elsewhere, buyers tend to gravitate toward floor plans that already incorporate the spaces that matter most to their lifestyle. That’s why offering a variety of thoughtfully designed floor plans is so important. It allows buyers to select a home that best fits their individual needs and preferences.

Looking ahead, how do you expect changing family structures and the way people live together to influence Traton’s next generation of floor plans?

As housing costs continue to put pressure on household budgets, we anticipate that multigenerational living will become an important consideration for home buyers. Sharing a home can offer financial advantages while allowing families to stay connected and support one another. We believe buyers will continue to place a premium on flexible floor plans that provide both shared gathering spaces and private retreats, allowing multiple generations to live comfortably under one roof. At Traton, our goal is to continue designing homes that reflect how families live today while anticipating how their needs may change in the years ahead.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5597. Penélope Cruz Reveals Why She and Javier Bardem Chose To Raise Their Children in Madrid

Penélope Cruz has lifted the lid on why she and her husband, Javier Bardem, prefer raising their two kids in Spain.

While speaking to The Perfect Magazine, the actress, 52, revealed that she and Bardem, 57, opted to bring their son Leo, 15, and daughter Luna, 12, up in Madrid because it allows them to live a more private lifestyle.

“All our families are there, and the friends from childhood and from our teenage years; it’s easier to have a normal life, you know?” Cruz told the outlet.

She added, “You have to make an effort to keep a part of your life private, but I think when you have children, it’s really important, and they deserve that, they completely deserve that."

The Hollywood A-lister noted that when her children get older, they can decide whether they want to be in the spotlight.

"Later they can decide what they want to do in terms of their work and everything. But they need to have that freedom and not be exposed to things when they are little," she explained.

Cruz and Bardem said "I do" in 2010. The couple tends to keep tight-lipped about their private life.

However, the star has previously opened up about their parenting style, telling Elle in 2024 that they do not allow their children to have cell phones.

“It’s so easy to be manipulated, especially if you have a brain that is still forming, and who pays the price? Not us, not our generation, who, maybe at 25, learned how a BlackBerry worked. It’s a cruel experiment on children, on teenagers," Cruz said.

Cruz previously told People that her kids "finally" considered her a cool mom after she met Bad Bunny.

She revealed that the family attended the singer's residency in Puerto Rico and have since been to five of his international tour shows.

“But the first one in Puerto Rico is when Benito came to me and asked me to go with him to say the ‘Acho, PR es otra cosa,’” Cruz said, referring to the opening line of the musician’s song “VOY A LLeVARTE PA PR.”

“And finally my kids came to me and said, ‘Mom, finally you we can say you are cool.' Thank you, Benito! It took me all these years,” she teased.

#5596. Commvault unveils Recovery Studio, AgentRecover update and joint work with three partners

Data protection provider Commvault Systems Inc. today used its SHIFT 2026 customer event to unveil Recovery Studio, a new service that will automate the rebuilding of entire business applications after an outage or cyberattack.

Four other announcements cover recovery for artificial intelligence agents and joint work with Databricks Inc., Nvidia Corp. and Zscaler Inc.

AgentRecover, the company’s tool for reversing damage done by AI agents, is being extended to agents built on Microsoft Corp.’s Foundry and on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore from Amazon Web Services Inc. Databricks and Nvidia technology will draw on governed enterprise data from Commvault’s Data Activate service. The Zscaler agreement is a strategic partnership centered on AI security.

Recovery Studio goes after the manual work of restoring a business one piece at a time. Data alone does not get an application running again. Without the identities, configurations and infrastructure it depends on, an application can stay offline long after its files are back.

A large enterprise may have hundreds of applications and thousands of identities to bring up in sequence. Getting back to even a minimal level of operation takes 28 days on average under conventional approaches, according to Commvault research from last year.

In place of that manual work, the service uses automated runbooks that rebuild and validate each component in order. Commvault said the runbooks also restore identity systems and cloud configurations, firewall rules included. Threat scans can run inside a runbook on supported resources, and the results feed into the call on whether a service is ready to go back into production. Operational, disaster and cyber recovery all run from the same platform.

Pranay Ahlawat, Commvault’s chief technology and AI officer, called the launch “the DevOps moment for recovery.” He said one orchestrated flow can take over from the spreadsheets and war rooms that recovery teams lean on today.

The AgentRecover update moves the company’s agent protection onto the platforms where businesses build production agents. In September Commvault added protection for agent configurations that tools such as Anthropic PBC’s Claude Code store on employee laptops.

Phil Goodwin, research vice president at International Data Corp., said conventional recovery assumes a discrete set of data at one point in time. Agents break that assumption, because the agent, its data and the resources around it all have to come back “at machine speed,” he said.

On Bedrock AgentCore and Foundry, the software discovers each agent and maps the data, applications and infrastructure it interacts with. If an agent goes rogue, its activity log shows which systems it may have touched across platforms.

Restores target the agent and whatever it changed. Customers can also run AgentRecover with Commvault’s identity recovery and change auditing tools to trace the identities an agent acted through.

The Databricks and Nvidia announcements both build on Data Activate, which turns backup copies protected by Commvault into datasets for analytics and AI. Much of the data companies hold is unstructured and scattered across systems. In research from BARC published by DataHub in June, 70% of data and AI leaders said less than half of their unstructured data could be found and used for AI.

Commvault Data Activate for Databricks shares data under Commvault management into Databricks through OpenSharing. The data arrives as governed tables in Unity Catalog with its ownership, access permissions and lineage intact.

Updates keep flowing as source content changes or is deleted, and customers do not have to rebuild a connection to every original source. Alan Atkinson, chief business development officer at Commvault, said the aim is “turning protected data into an active business asset.”

Nvidia’s part, delivered as a reference design for software-as-a-service and software deployments, centers on retrieval. Nvidia NIM microservices and Nemotron Retriever, together with the Nvidia cuVS library used with Apache Solr, extract and organize Commvault-protected content so applications and agents can pull from it more easily. Data Activate keeps that content current as source files change, retention periods expire or permissions are revoked.

On the security side, Commvault and Zscaler listed AI discovery, runtime governance and agent detection and recovery as early areas of collaboration, and the companies did not announce a joint product or availability date. Zscaler’s Security for AI line polices how employees and agents use AI tools. Dhawal Sharma, Zscaler’s executive vice president of AI security and strategic initiatives, said organizations need to be “prepared to recover quickly if something goes wrong.”

Recovery Studio, AgentRecover’s Amazon Bedrock AgentCore support and the Databricks integration are all due to enter early access in December, the last of them in select Microsoft Azure regions. Foundry support comes sooner, with early access targeted for this month.

The Nvidia reference design is set to reach general availability in 2027 after an early release in December. Recovery Studio will be priced on the amount of data configured for orchestrated recovery, and Commvault plans general availability in the coming months.

A virtual edition of SHIFT follows on Nov. 18.

#5595. Douglas Elliman Goes All-In for AI After Q3’s Flat Earnings

After a middling third quarter, Douglas Elliman CEO Michael Liebowitz told investors that recent changes and efforts to the company are to “modernize” and build a “more efficient platform” by early 2027.

The luxury brokerage’s revenue fell short in the third quarter at $252.1 million for 2026, a $10 million drop compared to 2025’s revenue of $262.8 million.

For the first nine months of the year, revenue also dropped and was reported at $749.9 million. In 2025, that revenue was reported at $787.6 million.

During the Q3 earnings call for Douglas Elliman, Liebowitz claimed that the last quarter was about “technological upgrades” and emphasized the company’s movement toward execution.

“Technology is central to our strategy, and the transformation we introduced last quarter has continued to advance as part of our broader efforts to modernize the business and reduce costs,” he stated.

The company has faced struggles both in the market and internally over the past two years, with C-suite turnover and competition in its home market of New York City.

After the earnings report, the company’s stock jumped 12%, though it is still down 30% this year.

Liebowitz also mentioned multiple additions to Douglas Elliman this past quarter, including Sharon Milz as head of AI technology transformation, Nick Patino as director of AI enablement and Jamie Gagliano as chief operations officer.

“Sharon is overseeing our enterprise AI strategy and deployment as well as the broader technology transformation across the company,” he added. “Nick focuses on making sure these capabilities become part of how we get things done across the company, translating new technology into adoption, productivity and measuring business value. Jamie brings significant experience working with agents and building businesses. She’s already looking across our national operations at how we simplify processes, strengthen support and build a more scalable organization.”

Have an opinion on this topic? Please submit a Letter to the Editor.

Aside from a drop in revenue, Douglas Elliman also reported a drop in operating income (loss) annually. For Q3 2026, the company reported an operating income of $6.3 million, while last year’s operating loss clocked in at $10.7 million.

Bryant Kirkland—Douglas Elliman’s CFO—stated on the Q3 earnings call, however, that the year-over-year comparisons lean negatively because of 2025’s data.

“The year-over-year comparisons for the nine months ended Sept. 30, 2026 are impacted by a difficult comparable, due to an unusually strong first quarter of 2025,” he noted.

Adjusted EBITDA—or earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization—may signal positive growth for the brokerage, as Q3’s EBITDA was $5.3 million compared to last year’s $1 million.

While the adjusted EBITDA grew for Q3, the company’s adjusted net loss greatly overshadows many gains, as it reported the adjusted net loss at nearly $8 million, compared to last year’s $1.4 million.

Existing-home sales, Kirkland mentioned, were up 1.9% from October 2026, compared to October 2025. But, this result was weighed down. October 2026 had one fewer sales day than last year, Kirkland said. In reality, the receipts from existing-home sales were down 2.7% in October 2026 compared to October 2025.

Liebowitz attributed many of the Q3 losses to changes, and called it a “growth stage.”

Kirkland claimed the company would see returns on its current investments—such as the development marketing pipeline of $26 billion and the additional $11.8 billion scheduled to come to market Dec. 31, 2027—between 2026 and 2032. In particular, Kirkland mentioned Florida’s real estate market and its marketing value.

“We see positive indicators within our development marketing business in Florida, with approximately $19.5 billion gross transaction value, of the $26 billion of gross transaction value that is being actively marketed,” he added. “For most projects in Florida, we receive progress payments during the marketing process and defer the related revenue and commission it spent until the earnings process is complete, which is when the underlying sale closes.”

After investing in an “AI transformation” last quarter, the Q3 earnings release noted that the initiative is expected to gradually drive significant savings in non-commission operating expenses over the next three years.

“Modernizing those systems should make the company more efficient while giving our agents and employees better tools and more time to focus on clients, relationships and growing their businesses,” Liebowitz claimed. “That work is underway, and we remain focused on gradually realizing meaningful efficiencies in our non-commission operating expenses beginning in 2027.”
